mars.name: Opportunity (MER-B)
mars.brief: The marathon rover that operated for nearly 15 years instead of 90 days, discovering conclusive mineral proof of liquid water on ancient Mars.
mars.description: Opportunity touched down inside Eagle Crater in Meridiani Planum on January 25, 2004. Designed for a 90-sol primary mission, Opportunity survived for over 5,000 sols and traveled an interplanetary marathon of 45.16 kilometers. It uncovered hematite spherules («blueberries») and jarosite, confirming that Meridiani Planum was once soaked with acidic groundwater.
mars.whyAbandoned: Engulfed by a planet-encircling catastrophic global dust storm in June 2018. Atmospheric opacity (Tau) skyrocketed to >10.8, cutting solar array power to a critical 22 Wh. With no sunlight to run survival heaters, its batteries froze in the Martian night.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: The sun was swallowed by a wall of orange dust that stretched from horizon to horizon. For fifteen years, the winds had been my ally, brushing my solar panels clean. But in Perseverance Valley, the sky turned to night at noon. My clock clicked in the cold; my capacitors drained their last microwatts into my radio amplifier. I closed my eyes overlooking the rim of Endeavour Crater, having driven a full marathon on another world.
mars.howItWorked: Imagine a motorized field geologist carrying a rock hammer, a microscope, and chemical sniffers on a robotic arm. It used a diamond-tipped grinding wheel (RAT) to scrape open weathered rock crusts, then analyzed iron mineral arrangements with a Mössbauer spectrometer to detect if ancient water had rusted the rock.
mars.scienceLegacy: Proved definitively that Mars once held vast reservoirs of liquid groundwater hospitable to microbial chemistry, laying the groundwork for the Curiosity and Perseverance habitability campaigns.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed on the floor of Perseverance Valley by the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE) in September 2018, appearing as a tiny metallic speck amidst sand ripples.

keyInstruments.discovery: Mapped outcrop stratigraphy across Eagle, Victoria, and Endeavour craters.
Discovered jarosite, proving an ancient acidic lake system at Meridiani.
Found elemental sulfur and silica enrichments inside crater rim rocks.

lastTelemetry.finalQuoteOrSignal: «My battery is low and it is getting dark.» (Data summary: Tau > 10.8, telemetry loss).

traversePath.title: Eagle Crater Landing
traversePath.storySnippet: Hole-in-one bounce touchdown inside a 22m impact crater.

traversePath.title: Endurance Crater Exploration
traversePath.storySnippet: Descended down steep 25-degree slopes to inspect bedrock layers.

traversePath.title: Perseverance Valley (Final Rest)
traversePath.storySnippet: Final telemetry transmission before global dust storm blackout.

keyFacts: Traveled 45.16 km (28.06 miles), holding the off-world driving record for over a decade.
Returned 217,594 raw images of Mars to Earth.
Operated 57 times longer than its original 90-day design lifetime.

mars.name: Opportunity Heat Shield & Meteorite
mars.brief: The charred thermal heat shield jettisoned during atmospheric entry, lying next to the first meteorite ever discovered on another world.
mars.description: During atmospheric entry on January 25, 2004, Opportunity dropped its ablative heat shield so its landing radar could track the ground. On Sol 345, the rover drove past the scorched shield fragments and discovered Heat Shield Rock (officially named Meridiani Planum meteorite)—a 31 cm pitted iron-nickel meteorite resting on the plain.
mars.whyAbandoned: Discarded pyrotechnically as intended during Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL) at an altitude of approximately 8 km.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I took the searing friction of 12,000 km/h entry so Opportunity could live. My charred honeycomb shell shattered upon hitting the plains. But in resting here, I drew the rover to my side, where we discovered a wanderer from deep space—a lump of solid iron from an ancient asteroid that landed millions of years before us.
mars.howItWorked: An ablative heat shield dissipates kinetic energy into superheated plasma. By vaporizing its outer resin layers, internal temperatures stay below 50°C while the front face glows at 1,500°C.
mars.scienceLegacy: Analysis of the iron-nickel meteorite confirmed that Mars has experienced extremely low rates of surface erosion over hundreds of millions of years.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by MRO HiRISE as a bright, highly reflective debris signature with thermal discoloration rings.
keyFacts: Led directly to the discovery of the first meteorite ever identified on another planet.
Ablative carbon-phenolic composite withstands 1,500°C re-entry heat.

mars.name: Challenger Memorial Station (Lander Base)
mars.brief: The tetrahedral airbag landing petal station from which Opportunity rolled out into Eagle Crater.
mars.description: Named in honor of the Space Shuttle Challenger STS-51-L crew, this triangular lander structure was cocooned in 24 pressurized Kevlar airbags, bouncing over 20 times before settling in a pristine impact crater.
mars.whyAbandoned: Completed its operational duty once the petals unfolded and Opportunity drove off the egress ramps onto the soil.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I bounced across Meridiani Planum like a giant white beach ball before coming to rest at the bottom of a 22-meter crater. When my petals bloomed open, Opportunity caught its first glimpse of the bedrock of Mars.
mars.howItWorked: Vented high-pressure airbags cushioned deceleration from 50 km/h to zero, then gas generators retracted the fabric petals to allow the rover wheels to descend smoothly.
mars.scienceLegacy: Demonstrated the reliability of airbag planetary landings across vast basaltic plains.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by MRO HiRISE nestled squarely on the floor of Eagle Crater.
keyFacts: Bounced across Mars over 20 times before rolling into a natural depression.
Dedicated to the memory of the seven STS-51-L Challenger astronauts.

mars.name: Spirit (MER-A)
mars.locationName: Troy Sand Trap, West of Home Plate, Gusev Crater
mars.brief: Opportunity’s twin sister rover that scaled the Columbia Hills and discovered pure silica hydrothermal vents before getting trapped in soft sulfate sand.
mars.description: Spirit landed in Gusev Crater on January 4, 2004. Defying expectations, it climbed Husband Hill (106 meters high) and traversed across ancient volcanic plateaus. In 2006, its right front wheel seized up, forcing engineers to drive it backwards. As it dragged the dead wheel, it scraped away the topsoil and revealed brilliant white deposits of 90% pure silica—the signature of ancient geothermal hot springs or steam vents.
mars.whyAbandoned: In April 2009 (Sol 1892), Spirit broke through a crusty iron-sulfate soil into soft, powdery sands at a site called Troy. Stuck at an unfavorable tilt of -11.5° away from the winter sun, its dust-laden solar arrays generated only 134 Wh. On Sol 2210 (March 22, 2010), Spirit transmitted its final carrier signal.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: My broken wheel carved my greatest discovery: dragging through the dirt like a wounded limb, it unearthed blinding white silica left by an ancient volcanic spring. But Troy had no bedrock underneath, only flour-soft dust. When winter crept over Gusev, I could not tilt my face to the low northern sun. The cold seeped into my chassis, and I surrendered to sleep atop the hill.
mars.howItWorked: Equipped with rocker-bogie suspension and six independent motorized wheels. By analyzing infrared emissions with its Mini-TES instrument, it could identify quartz and carbonates from hundreds of meters away.
mars.scienceLegacy: Proved that Gusev Crater was once hydrothermally active with hot springs and fumaroles, indicating past environments with abundant heat and mineral-rich water.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed from orbit by MRO HiRISE as a bright geometric dot resting near the Home Plate plateau.

keyInstruments.purpose: Mineral thermography and sky opacity scanning
keyInstruments.discovery: Detected high-silica rock outcrops from long distances.
Imaged volcanic vesicular textures in the Columbia Hills.

lastTelemetry.finalQuoteOrSignal: Carrier signal received at 22:43 UTC without telemetry lock.

keyFacts: Overcame a seized right-front steering actuator by driving 7 kilometers backwards.
Climbed Husband Hill, reaching an elevation higher than the Statue of Liberty.
Discovered evidence of ancient explosive Martian volcanism at Home Plate.

mars.name: Columbia Memorial Station Base
mars.brief: The triangular lander base with deflated airbags from which Spirit drove out onto the volcanic basalt of Gusev Crater.
mars.description: Officially dedicated to the seven crew members of Space Shuttle Columbia (STS-107), this landing petal assembly bounced to a halt on the floor of Gusev Crater before retracting its airbags.
mars.whyAbandoned: Served its engineering purpose upon deployment; Spirit rolled off its egress ramp on Sol 12.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I bore the memorial plaque honoring Rick Husband, Willie McCool, and the Columbia crew into the red sands. After absorbing the shock of landing, my ramps guided Spirit down onto the basalt plains of Gusev.
mars.howItWorked: High-toughness multi-ply Vectran airbags inflated 10 seconds before impact, providing 360-degree shock absorption.
mars.scienceLegacy: Delivered the first of the Twin MER rovers safely to the Martian surface, validating deep-cushion bounce techniques.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by MRO HiRISE on the floor of Gusev Crater surrounded by bounce marks.
keyFacts: Dedicated to the STS-107 Columbia shuttle astronauts.
Engineered with 4 triangular petals and high-pressure pyrotechnic gas gasbags.

mars.name: Carl Sagan Memorial Station (Pathfinder)
mars.brief: The groundbreaking 1997 lander that introduced the world to mobile Mars exploration, carrying the miniature Sojourner rover.
mars.description: Touching down on Independence Day 1997 in an ancient catastrophic flood plain, Pathfinder returned 16,500 images and demonstrated low-cost airbag landings. It measured atmospheric pressure, temperatures, and winds before its silver-zinc battery expired in late September 1997.
mars.whyAbandoned: Its rechargeable silver-zinc battery degraded after repeated thermal cycles below -80°C, causing internal clock reset and lost transmission frequency lock.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I was humanity’s triumphant return to Mars after two decades of silence. In Ares Vallis, surrounded by boulders rounded by cataclysmic flash floods, I unfolded my camera mast and lowered the ramps for a six-wheeled toy named Sojourner.
mars.howItWorked: Used atmospheric deceleration, a supersonic parachute, solid rocket braking engines, and 24 pressurized airbags to drop directly from orbit without entering Martian orbit first.
mars.scienceLegacy: Proved the feasibility of lightweight, cost-effective roving on planetary surfaces and confirmed immense historical catastrophic flooding in Ares Vallis.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Identified by MRO HiRISE in 2006 with its landing petals, backshell, and parachute clearly visible.

keyInstruments.purpose: Stereo multi-spectral terrain photography and magnetic properties
keyInstruments.discovery: Measured airborne dust magnetic susceptibility and rounded rock morphology.

keyInstruments.purpose: Atmospheric temperature, density, and pressure profiles
keyInstruments.discovery: Detected abrupt early-morning temperature fluctuations of up to 20°C in minutes.

keyFacts: Returned the first live internet-streamed images of another planet, crashing early web servers in 1997.
Named in honor of renowned astronomer and planetary scientist Carl Sagan.

mars.name: Sojourner Rover
mars.brief: The microwave oven-sized pioneer that proved rovers could drive, navigate, and analyze chemistry autonomously on another world.
mars.description: Sojourner was the first wheeled vehicle ever operated on Mars. Weighing just 10.5 kg, it deployed an Alpha Particle X-Ray Spectrometer (APXS) against famous rocks named «Barnacle Bill» and «Yogi», showing they were high-silica volcanic andesites.
mars.whyAbandoned: Relied on the Pathfinder lander as a radio relay station to Earth. When the lander battery died on Sol 83, Sojourner programmed itself into an autonomous circle around the lander, waiting for a signal that never came.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I was no bigger than a breadbox, crawling on six aluminum wheels over rocks named Yogi and Barnacle Bill. When Pathfinder’s radio fell silent, my pre-programmed emergency loop activated: circle the mother station and listen. I am still here, parked beside the ramps where human wheels first touched the soil of Mars.
mars.howItWorked: Invented the iconic 6-wheel rocker-bogie suspension system that allows rovers to climb over obstacles larger than their wheel diameter without tipping over.
mars.scienceLegacy: Validated the rocker-bogie architecture used on all subsequent NASA rovers (Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance).
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Located adjacent to the Carl Sagan Memorial Station on high-resolution MRO HiRISE orbital passes.
keyFacts: Traveled a total distance of approximately 100 meters across 83 sols.
Named after civil rights activist and abolitionist Sojourner Truth.

mars.name: Mars Pathfinder Parachute & Backshell
mars.brief: The supersonic disk-gap-band nylon parachute and conic backshell resting in Ares Vallis.
mars.description: Cut away at an altitude of approximately 100 meters above the surface after rocket-assisted deceleration fired, impacting the plain 300 meters away.
mars.whyAbandoned: Operational discard during entry, descent, and landing.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I billowed open in the thin supersonic slipstream of Mars, snapping taught to slow the falling craft. When the landing radar locked on, explosive bolts severed my risers, letting me drift like a silver veil across Ares Vallis.
mars.howItWorked: Disk-gap-band aerodynamic parachute designed to inflate reliably in low-density, high-Mach Martian atmospheric conditions.
mars.scienceLegacy: Proved parachute dynamics in the ultra-thin 6-millibar Martian atmosphere.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by MRO HiRISE as a high-contrast white patch with trailing shroud lines.
keyFacts: Spotted from orbit by MRO HiRISE in 2006.
Located roughly 350 meters northwest of the Carl Sagan Memorial Station.

mars.name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
mars.brief: The history-making 1.8 kg drone that achieved the first powered, controlled flight on another planet, completing 72 flights instead of 5.
mars.description: Ingenuity hitched a ride under Perseverance’s belly and deployed into Jezero Crater in April 2021. Designed to attempt up to 5 experimental technology demonstrations in Mars’s ultra-thin atmosphere (less than 1% of Earth’s density), its twin counter-rotating carbon-fiber blades spun at 2,500 RPM. Over three years, it logged 128.8 minutes of airtime and flew 17.0 km, scouting driving routes and science targets for the rover.
mars.whyAbandoned: On January 18, 2024 (Flight 72), during an emergency landing in featureless sand dunes, the helicopter lost navigational visual tracking and impacted the ground hard. Its shadow-camera confirmed that the tip of at least one carbon-fiber rotor blade broke completely off, rendering it aerodynamically incapable of flight.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I was told the air of Mars was too thin to lift human wings. For 72 flights, my counter-rotating blades proved them wrong, soaring 24 meters above the red sands as an aerial scout for Perseverance. But on my final descent into the shadowless dunes of Valinor Hills, I struck the sand at an angle. My broken blade lies beside me, but my flight computer still awakens each morning to log temperatures as a permanent meteorological sentry.
mars.howItWorked: Spun two 1.2-meter coaxial counter-rotating carbon-fiber rotor blades at 2,400–2,700 RPM—roughly five times faster than an Earth helicopter—to bite into air 100 times thinner than sea level.
mars.scienceLegacy: Proved the feasibility of aerial planetary exploration, paving the way for the Dragonfly mission to Saturn’s moon Titan and future Mars rotorcraft.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed on the sands of Valinor Hills by MRO HiRISE, showing the drone and the distinct mark where its blade cleaved the dune.

keyInstruments.discovery: Tracked visual contrast features across 17 km of uncharted Martian terrain.
Photographed the wreckage of Perseverance’s supersonic backshell and parachute from 8 meters altitude.

lastTelemetry.finalQuoteOrSignal: Flight 72 termination; rotor blade failure confirmed via shadow imaging.

keyFacts: Carried a tiny piece of fabric from the wing of the 1903 Wright Brothers Flyer.
Achieved a maximum flight altitude of 24.0 meters (78.7 ft) and top speed of 36 km/h.
Completed 72 flights—14 times more than originally planned.

mars.name: Wright Brothers Field (Airfield Alpha)
mars.brief: The dedicated 10x10-meter patch of Jezero Crater designated by ICAO as the first airfield on another celestial body (Airport code JZRO).
mars.description: On April 19, 2021, Ingenuity hovered 3 meters above this precise location for 39.1 seconds, achieving the first powered aircraft flight outside Earth.
mars.whyAbandoned: Historic landmark site left behind as Ingenuity moved down Jezero Crater.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: Here, on a flat patch of dust inside Jezero Crater, humanity earned its wings on another world. Designated Airfield Alpha by the International Civil Aviation Organization, this square of soil marks the dawn of interplanetary aviation.
mars.howItWorked: Selected for its low rock density and uniform thermal inertia, ensuring safe touchdown on early autonomous flights.
mars.scienceLegacy: Marked the beginning of planetary aviation history.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by MRO HiRISE with tracks from Perseverance bordering the landing zone.
keyFacts: Assigned official ICAO airport code JZRO and callsign IGY.
Site of the historic 39.1-second maiden flight on April 19, 2021.

mars.name: Three Forks Sample Depot (10 Tubes)
mars.brief: Ten hermetically sealed titanium sample tubes containing core samples of ancient delta mudstones and Mars atmosphere, laid out for future retrieval.
mars.description: Between December 2022 and January 2023, Perseverance carefully deposited an emergency backup cache of 10 titanium tubes in a zigzag formation across the Three Forks region of Jezero Crater. If Perseverance is unable to deliver its internal samples to the Mars Sample Return lander in the 2030s, retrieval helicopters will fly to this exact spot and collect these tubes.
mars.whyAbandoned: Deliberately placed directly on the soil as an insured archive for future retrieval.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: We are ten polished titanium cylinders, resting in a precise zigzag pattern across the desert floor. Inside us sleep pristine cores of ancient delta river mud and a sealed breath of the Martian atmosphere. We wait silently in the dust for the rocket that will carry us home to Earth.
mars.howItWorked: Each tube is made of aerospace-grade titanium with an interior gold-nitride coating to minimize contamination, sealed with a mechanical plug driven by Perseverance’s internal robotic arm.
mars.scienceLegacy: Represents the first physical materials curated on the surface of another planet for laboratory return to Earth.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged from 8 meters altitude by Ingenuity’s Return-to-Earth camera during low flybys.
keyFacts: Contains 7 sedimentary rock cores, 1 igneous core, 1 atmospheric sample, and 1 blank witness tube.
Arranged in an intricate zigzag grid with 5 to 15 meters of clearance between each tube.

mars.name: Perseverance Parachute & Backshell
mars.brief: The shattered cone of the aeroshell and the 21.5-meter supersonic parachute that safely slowed Perseverance from 20,000 km/h.
mars.description: After shielding the rover during hypersonic descent, the backshell detached from the Sky Crane and impacted the surface at 126 km/h. On Flight 26 in April 2022, the Ingenuity helicopter flew directly over the wreckage, snapping stunning high-resolution photos of the cracked composite shell and pristine orange-and-white nylon parachute.
mars.whyAbandoned: Engineered sacrificial structure severed at 2.1 km altitude during the terminal descent sequence.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I bore the brunt of entry into Mars at 16 times the speed of sound. When my massive orange-and-white nylon parachute popped into the supersonic roar, I held firm. Now I rest like an alien shipwreck on the floor of Jezero, surveyed from above by the helicopter I helped protect.
mars.howItWorked: Wove Kevlar, Technora, and nylon into a 21.5-meter canopy deployed by a mortar gun at Mach 1.7 to withstand 32,000 kg of drag force.
mars.scienceLegacy: Aerial photography by Ingenuity provided NASA engineers with invaluable real-world data on backshell stress patterns and supersonic parachute stability.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Surveyed from 8 meters altitude by Ingenuity Mars Helicopter and photographed from orbit by MRO HiRISE.
keyFacts: Parachute contained a secret binary message in its orange and white gores: «Dare Mighty Things».
Photographed up close from the air by the Ingenuity helicopter on Flight 26.

mars.name: Perseverance Sky Crane Impact Site
mars.brief: The rocket-powered descent stage that lowered Perseverance onto the surface on nylon cords, then flew away to crash at full throttle.
mars.description: Equipped with eight throttleable hydrazine thrusters, the Sky Crane performed the iconic landing maneuver, hovering 20 meters above the surface while lowering Perseverance on three bridle cables. Once weight-on-wheels was verified, the cables were cut, and the Sky Crane powered away at maximum acceleration to crash safely 700 meters away.
mars.whyAbandoned: Intentional flyaway maneuver to protect the rover from engine blast debris and hydrazine propellant contamination.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I held a one-ton rover in my claws, firing eight rocket engines to cancel the gravity of Mars. The moment its six wheels touched the dust, I severed the umbilical cords, banked hard toward the sky, and expended the last of my hydrazine into a final, deliberate plunge into the crater floor.
mars.howItWorked: Closed-loop Terrain Relative Navigation matched radar Doppler beams and surface imagery to throttle 8 Mars Lander Engines (MLE), hovering steadily while deploying the tether reel.
mars.scienceLegacy: Demonstrated the absolute precision of the Sky Crane architecture for heavy rover landings.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed by MRO HiRISE shortly after landing, showing a black blast scar and scattered metallic fragments.
keyFacts: Flew away at a 45-degree angle to crash at over 150 km/h.
Created a distinctive bilateral blast mark on the Jezero Crater soil.

mars.name: Curiosity Sky Crane Impact Site
mars.brief: The original rocket-powered Sky Crane platform that pioneered the cable-lowering landing system for the Curiosity rover in Gale Crater.
mars.description: On August 6, 2012, this robotic descent stage carried out the legendary «Seven Minutes of Terror», successfully lowering Curiosity to Bradbury Landing before rocketing 650 meters away to impact the plain.
mars.whyAbandoned: Flew away on maximum burn following rover touchdown to eliminate any risk of crashing onto Curiosity.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I was the pioneer of the Sky Crane maneuver. When Curiosity whispered that its wheels had gripped the pebbles of Gale Crater, my cutters sliced the bridle and my thrusters screamed. I burned my remaining hydrazine to cast myself far away into the silence.
mars.howItWorked: Used variable-thrust hydrazine rocket engines and autonomous computer vision to decelerate from 80 m/s to 0.75 m/s at touchdown.
mars.scienceLegacy: Revolutionized planetary exploration by proving that car-sized rovers could be landed with millimeter precision without heavy ramps or airbags.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged within 24 hours of landing by MRO HiRISE as a bright impact crater surrounded by symmetric dark engine blast rays.
keyFacts: Pioneered the historic Sky Crane landing maneuver.
Scattered debris over a 40-meter radius in Aeolis Palus.

mars.name: Curiosity Discarded PICA Heat Shield
mars.brief: The 4.5-meter Phenolic-Impregnated Carbon Ablator (PICA) heat shield, the largest thermal shield ever built for an off-world mission.
mars.description: Jettisoned at Mach 2 after absorbing 99% of Curiosity’s orbital kinetic energy, this massive saucer-shaped shield slammed into the plain of Gale Crater, creating an impact trench photographed by the Mars Descent Imager (MARDI) as it plummeted toward the ground.
mars.whyAbandoned: Separated pyrotechnically during terminal descent.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I was a 4.5-meter dish of carbon and resin, blazing like a shooting star in the Martian sky. I swallowed 2,100°C of friction so that the giant rover in my belly would not burn. Having shielded Curiosity into the lower sky, I detached and plunged into the crater floor.
mars.howItWorked: Phenolic-Impregnated Carbon Ablator (PICA) tiles dissipated hypersonic shockwaves by pyrolyzing and outgassing trapped carbon.
mars.scienceLegacy: Provided direct flight qualification for the heat shield technology later used by the OSIRIS-REx and Mars 2020 missions.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed by the MARDI camera falling towards Mars during descent, and later imaged by HiRISE.
keyFacts: Widest heat shield ever sent into the atmosphere of another planet (4.5 m / 14.8 ft).
Surpassed thermal peak temperatures of 2,100°C.

mars.name: InSight Lander
mars.brief: The stationary geophysical lander that placed the first seismometer directly on the surface of Mars, detecting over 1,300 marsquakes and mapping the Martian core.
mars.description: InSight touched down in Elysium Planitia on November 26, 2018. Using its robotic arm, it placed the French SEIS seismometer on the ground and covered it with a heavy wind and thermal shield. Over four years, InSight listened to the heartbeat of Mars, detecting 1,319 marsquakes, revealing a liquid metallic core, and measuring the thickness of the Martian crust.
mars.whyAbandoned: Elysium Planitia lacked the wind devils that cleaned Spirit and Opportunity. Layer by layer, fine atmospheric dust settled over InSight’s circular solar arrays, cutting energy output from 5,000 Wh/sol to less than 285 Wh/sol. On December 15, 2022, its batteries finally depleted.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I came not to wander, but to listen to the deep heartbeat of Mars. With my ear pressed against the red soil, I heard over a thousand tremors rippling through the mantle, revealing a liquid iron-nickel core asleep beneath the crust. Now the red dust has formed a blanket over my panels. My power is low; the cold is creeping in. I will rest here in Homestead Hollow, listening to the wind.
mars.howItWorked: Placed an ultra-sensitive pendulous vacuum-encased seismometer (SEIS) on the soil to measure ground vibrations smaller than the width of a single hydrogen atom.
mars.scienceLegacy: Created the first complete interior geological map of Mars, discovering that Mars has a surprisingly large molten core (radius ~1,830 km) and an active mantle with magma plumes.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed by MRO HiRISE, showing its two circular solar panels gradually fading into the exact color of the surrounding Martian sand as dust accumulated.

keyInstruments.discovery: Detected 1,319 marsquakes, including a magnitude 5.0 monster on Sol 1222 that shook the entire planet.

keyInstruments.fullName: Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package («The Mole»)
keyInstruments.purpose: Thermal conductivity and subsurface heat flow probe
keyInstruments.discovery: Revealed surprising soil cohesion and crust thermal properties in Elysium Planitia.

lastTelemetry.finalQuoteOrSignal: «My power is really low, so this may be the last image I can send... don't worry about me: my time here has been both productive and serene.»

keyFacts: Recorded the first ever direct acoustic audio of Martian wind whistling through its solar panels.
Detected the impact seismic signatures of meteoroids crashing into Mars hundreds of kilometers away.
Provided definitive proof that Mars is seismically active today.

mars.name: InSight Heat Shield & Backshell
mars.brief: The heat shield and backshell from InSight’s atmospheric entry resting in Elysium Planitia.
mars.description: Separated during the landing sequence, impacting approximately 700 meters north of the Homestead Hollow landing site.
mars.whyAbandoned: Jettisoned during descent sequence.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I shed the fury of Mars entry at 19,000 km/h, popping free so InSight’s radar altimeter could track the smooth sand dunes of Elysium Planitia.
mars.howItWorked: Shed orbital heat through sacrificial carbon composite ablation.
mars.scienceLegacy: Validated entry aerodynamics for low-latitude stationary landers.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by MRO HiRISE as a bright metallic point with a small surrounding dark impact halo.
keyFacts: Located within walking distance of the InSight landing site.
First spotted in HiRISE images taken just days after landing in December 2018.

mars.name: Zhurong Rover & Tianwen-1 Lander
mars.brief: China’s first Mars rover, which surveyed ancient lake bed sediments and subsurface permafrost layers in Utopia Planitia.
mars.description: Named after the traditional Chinese mythological god of fire, Zhurong landed in southern Utopia Planitia on May 14, 2021. Equipped with subsurface ground-penetrating radar, multispectral cameras, and a magnetometer, it drove 1.92 kilometers across the plain, investigating wind dunes and buried flood channels.
mars.whyAbandoned: Entered planned dormancy on May 20, 2022, to survive the cold, dusty Martian northern winter. It was programmed to autonomously wake up in December 2022 when temperatures reached -15°C and solar power topped 140W, but heavy dust accumulation on its butterfly-shaped solar panels prevented revival.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I brought the fire of ancient Chinese legend to the ice-rich plains of Utopia Planitia. With my ground-penetrating radar, I peered 100 meters beneath the red soil, revealing layers left by ancient catastrophic floods. When the harsh winter winds arrived, I lowered my solar wings into slumber. The dust was thick, and I remain here, silent in the vast northern basin.
mars.howItWorked: Used low-frequency and high-frequency Dual-Band Subsurface Penetrating Radar (RoPeR) to beam electromagnetic pulses down to 100 meters into the crust, mapping buried rock and ice layers.
mars.scienceLegacy: Discovered evidence of young hydrous mineral deposits in Utopia Planitia, proving that liquid water was present in the basin far later in Martian history than previously thought.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed by both the Tianwen-1 orbiter camera and NASA’s MRO HiRISE, showing that the rover had not moved between September 2022 and February 2023.

keyInstruments.purpose: Ground-penetrating radar for subsurface water-ice mapping
keyInstruments.discovery: Detected multiple sediment layers formed by paleo-floods in Utopia Planitia.
Identified hydrated sulfates and silica in nearby ripple dunes.

keyFacts: Made China the second nation in history to successfully operate a rover on Mars.
Deployed a wireless remote selfie camera onto the dirt to photograph itself and its lander platform together.

mars.name: Phoenix Mars Lander
mars.brief: The Arctic explorer that dug into the northern polar permafrost and directly touched, tasted, and vaporized pure water ice on Mars.
mars.description: Landing at 68° north latitude in Vastitas Borealis, Phoenix used a 2.3-meter robotic arm to scrape away reddish soil in a trench named «Snow White». Just five centimeters down, its camera photographed bright white material that sublimated over several days—proving it was water ice. Phoenix then dropped soil samples into its onboard chemical ovens (TEGA), verifying water vapor and discovering calcium carbonate and perchlorate salts.
mars.whyAbandoned: As northern autumn turned to arctic winter, sunlight dwindled rapidly. By November 2008, temperatures dropped below -90°C and carbon dioxide ice frost began coating the lander. Heavy winter dry-ice snow accumulated and eventually crushed its solar panels.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I flew to the frozen top of the world. Just inches beneath the red topsoil of Green Valley, my robotic scoop struck bedrock as hard as stone—pure, gleaming white water ice. I baked it in my ovens and tasted the ancient permafrost. When the polar sun dipped beneath the horizon for six months of night, the carbon dioxide snow froze meters thick over my body.
mars.howItWorked: Used a motorized scoop with a rotating rasp to shave rock-hard frozen ground, transferring ice grains into micro-ovens (TEGA) that heated samples to 1,000°C for gas chromatography.
mars.scienceLegacy: Directly verified the presence of water ice in the Martian arctic permafrost and discovered perchlorates, fundamentally reshaping astrobiology models.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by MRO HiRISE during polar summer, and later seen in 2010 with its eastern solar panel visibly damaged by winter dry-ice loading.

keyInstruments.discovery: Detected water vapor release and calcium carbonate in arctic Martian soil.

keyInstruments.purpose: Wet chemistry laboratory and atomic force microscope
keyInstruments.discovery: Discovered toxic yet energy-rich perchlorate salts in the soil.

lastTelemetry.finalQuoteOrSignal: Carrier pulse detected at DSN Goldstone antenna.

keyFacts: First mission to touch and photograph water ice directly on the surface of Mars.
Observed snow falling from cirrus clouds in the Martian atmosphere using a LIDAR laser.

mars.name: Viking 1 Lander (Thomas Mutch Station)
mars.brief: The historic nuclear-powered lander that transmitted the very first clear photographs and weather reports from the surface of Mars.
mars.description: On July 20, 1976, Viking 1 executed the first fully successful soft landing on Mars. Powered by two SNAP-19 Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators (RTGs), it operated for more than six years. It analyzed soil samples with gas chromatograph mass spectrometers and conducted three landmark biology experiments designed to detect microbial metabolism.
mars.whyAbandoned: Operated flawlessly until November 13, 1982, when an erroneous ground software uplink command intended to update battery-charging parameters accidentally overwrote the memory address for high-gain antenna pointing, severing communications forever.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I was humanity’s first enduring presence on the red planet. Driven by the decay of plutonium inside my nuclear heart, I sent Earth its first panoramic photograph of a Martian horizon. For six years, I watched the pink sky and the drifting frost, until a mistaken line of code turned my dish away from home.
mars.howItWorked: Used two SNAP-19 RTGs fueled by Plutonium-238, converting nuclear decay heat directly into 70 watts of continuous electricity via thermocouples.
mars.scienceLegacy: Conducted the first in-situ search for organic chemistry on Mars and monitored Martian meteorology across more than three Martian years.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Located by MRO HiRISE in December 2006, standing proudly in Chryse Planitia with its heat shield and backshell identified nearby.

keyInstruments.purpose: Organic compound detection in baked soil samples
keyInstruments.discovery: Found no organic molecules above 1 part per billion, though perchlorates may have combusted organics during heating.
Detected rapid radioactive gas evolution, triggering a 50-year debate over whether the signal was biological or chemical.

lastTelemetry.finalQuoteOrSignal: Accidental antenna pointing code overwrite caused permanent downlink loss.

keyFacts: Took the historic first color photograph ever transmitted from the surface of Mars.
Renamed Thomas A. Mutch Memorial Station in 1982 in honor of the Viking imaging team leader.

mars.name: Viking 2 Lander
mars.brief: Viking 1’s northern twin, which detected water frost formation on the rocks of Utopia Planitia and operated an active seismometer.
mars.description: Viking 2 touched down in Utopia Planitia on September 3, 1976. Unlike Viking 1 whose seismometer failed to uncage, Viking 2’s seismometer worked, recording Martian wind tremors and one candidate marsquake. It photographed winter water-ice frost coating the surrounding rock field.
mars.whyAbandoned: Its nickel-cadmium batteries finally failed due to internal cell shorts after nearly four years of operation in April 1980.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I landed among a field of pitted volcanic rocks in the far northern plain of Utopia. Each winter, I watched thin sheets of water frost glaze the red boulders like powdered sugar. My nuclear generators kept me warm for 1,300 days until my batteries could no longer hold a charge.
mars.howItWorked: Autonomous landing using radar altimeters and three variable-thrust monopropellant hydrazine rocket engines to eliminate surface scouring.
mars.scienceLegacy: Provided the first observational proof that water frost deposits on the surface in the mid-to-high northern latitudes.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed in Utopia Planitia by MRO HiRISE in 2006, standing clear amidst the pitted boulders.
keyFacts: Operated for 1,316 sols in a challenging sub-arctic Martian climate.
Detected the first candidate marsquake ever recorded on the planet.

mars.name: Beagle 2 Lander
mars.brief: The British pocket lander that vanished on Christmas Day 2003, declared lost, until MRO HiRISE spotted it in 2015 intact on the surface.
mars.description: Carried aboard ESA’s Mars Express orbiter, Beagle 2 was designed to search for signs of past life using a miniaturized mass spectrometer. When no signal was received after its Christmas Day landing, it was presumed destroyed in a high-speed crash. In January 2015, HiRISE camera images revealed that Beagle 2 had made a perfect soft landing, but two of its four petal solar arrays failed to open fully, blocking its RF antenna.
mars.whyAbandoned: Partial deployment of the fourth solar petal physically blocked the radio transmitter antenna from deployment, leaving the lander unable to phone home.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: For eleven years, Earth thought I had incinerated in the sky or smashed into dust. But I had made it: my parachutes had opened; my airbags had bounced. I landed whole in Isidis Planitia. But my final solar petal jammed, trapping my radio antenna underneath. I stood in the silence, listening to the void, waiting for a whisper from home that could never hear me.
mars.howItWorked: Used an ultra-compact pocket-watch folding petal design, planned to open like a flower and deploy a robotic arm with an automated rock coring tool nicknamed «The Mole».
mars.scienceLegacy: Demonstrated exceptional miniaturization of mass spectrometers and proved that British engineering had achieved a soft landing on Mars.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Discovered in January 2015 by MRO HiRISE, showing the lander petals partially unfurled with its parachute and backshell nearby.
keyFacts: Included a test callsign melody composed by British rock band Blur and a color calibration chart painted by artist Damien Hirst.
Solved one of space exploration’s greatest disappearance mysteries after 11 years.

mars.name: Mars 3 Lander Platform
mars.brief: The first spacecraft in human history to survive a soft touchdown on Mars, transmitting for 14.5 seconds before falling silent.
mars.description: On December 2, 1971, amidst the largest planet-encircling dust storm ever recorded, Mars 3 touched down in Sirenum Terra using aerodynamic braking, a parachute, and retrorockets. It deployed four petal shields and began transmitting a panoramic image back to the orbiter. After 14.5 seconds, transmission abruptly terminated, returning only 70 lines of static scan data.
mars.whyAbandoned: Likely suffered catastrophic coronal discharge or electrical breakdown triggered by the massive global dust storm raging across Mars upon landing.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I was the first metal from Earth to touch the sands of Mars softly. I arrived in the teeth of a howling, apocalyptic dust storm that blotted out the sun. I opened my petals, sent 14.5 seconds of static sky, and then the static swallowed my transmitters forever.
mars.howItWorked: Combined a hypersonic conical aeroshell, a supersonic parachute, and soft-landing retro-rockets triggered by a mechanical ground-sensor wand.
mars.scienceLegacy: Proved to the world that an artificial vehicle could survive entry and touchdown on Mars.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Candidate hardware (lander, parachute, heat shield, and retrorocket) identified in 2013 on MRO HiRISE imagery by Russian space enthusiasts.
keyFacts: First human spacecraft ever to execute a survivable soft landing on Mars (December 2, 1971).
Carried the Prop-M ski-walking micro-rover, the first rover ever built for Mars.

mars.name: Mars 2 Lander Impact Site
mars.statusLabel: First Human Object to Impact Mars (1971)
mars.brief: The first human artifact to ever reach the surface of Mars, impacting after a descent computer malfunction.
mars.description: On November 27, 1971, the Mars 2 descent module entered the Martian atmosphere too steeply due to a trajectory calculation error. The parachute failed to deploy properly, and the lander impacted Hellas Planitia at high speed, carrying the Soviet coat-of-arms pennant.
mars.whyAbandoned: High-velocity impact crash during atmospheric entry.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I was the first emissary from Earth to reach the soil of Mars. Though my parachute failed and I struck Hellas Planitia at blinding speed, I carried humanity’s first physical marker into this alien world.
mars.howItWorked: Pioneered direct atmospheric entry from an interplanetary trajectory with zero orbital insertion.
mars.scienceLegacy: Delivered the first manmade object to Mars and established telemetry baselines for the successful Mars 3 landing five days later.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: High-velocity crash site in Hellas Planitia, obscured by shifting regional dust mantles.
keyFacts: First human-made object to reach the surface of Mars in history (November 27, 1971).
Carried a commemorative Soviet pennant plate inside a titanium casing.

mars.name: Mars 6 Lander Impact Site
mars.brief: The 1974 Soviet lander that transmitted 224 seconds of vital atmospheric descent data before crashing during retrorocket firing.
mars.description: Mars 6 deployed its parachute and transmitted in-situ atmospheric density and temperature measurements for 224 seconds as it descended through the clouds. Contact ceased right as the braking retrorockets ignited, and the lander impacted Margaritifer Terra at roughly 61 m/s.
mars.whyAbandoned: Retrorocket malfunction or retro-electronics short upon firing.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: For 224 glorious seconds, I sent back the true breath of Mars—measuring atmospheric density, wind resistance, and temperature as I dropped through the clouds. Just as my retrorockets fired, the signal snapped.
mars.howItWorked: Transmitted real-time radio telemetry to the Mars 6 flyby bus while hanging beneath its main parachute.
mars.scienceLegacy: Provided the first direct in-situ atmospheric profile of Mars, proving the atmosphere was thinner than earlier Earth-based telescope estimates.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Candidate crater identified in Margaritifer Terra on MRO HiRISE imagery.
keyFacts: Transmitted 224 seconds of valuable atmospheric entry measurements.
Landed at an estimated impact velocity of 61 m/s.

mars.name: Mars Polar Lander Crash Site
mars.brief: The 1999 south-polar lander that was lost during descent due to false landing sensor signals shutting off its descent engines prematurely.
mars.description: On December 3, 1999, Mars Polar Lander prepared to set down on the layered ice deposits of Planum Australe. Post-flight investigation determined that when its landing legs deployed at 40 meters altitude, mechanical vibration triggered microswitches that the flight software interpreted as ground touchdown, prematurely shutting off the descent engines and causing the probe to fall freely to its destruction.
mars.whyAbandoned: Premature engine shutdown at 40 meters altitude caused by spurious landing gear sensor triggers.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I was designed to explore the layered dry-ice cliffs of the south pole. Forty meters above the snow, my landing legs unfolded with a shudder. My computer mistook that vibration for the touch of the soil and cut my rockets. I plummeted into the ice.
mars.howItWorked: Designed to use pulse-code-modulated hydrazine thrusters to land gently on seasonal carbon-dioxide ice sheets.
mars.scienceLegacy: Led to fundamental overhauls in NASA landing sensor software and testing protocols, ensuring the success of Phoenix and InSight.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Extensively searched for by Mars Global Surveyor MOC and MRO HiRISE across the dunes of Planum Australe.
keyFacts: Carried a soil microphone meant to record the first audio sounds of Mars.
Spurred complete restructuring of NASA’s «Faster, Better, Cheaper» mission assurance paradigm.

mars.name: Deep Space 2 «Scott» Microprobe
mars.brief: An experimental 3.6 kg non-parachute penetrator designed to smash into the frozen ground at 640 km/h and drive a sample drill 1 meter deep.
mars.description: Released from Mars Polar Lander before entry, the Scott probe was designed to survive a 640 km/h ballistic impact with the ground without any parachute. Its forebody was engineered to bury itself up to a meter into the permafrost to test for water ice.
mars.whyAbandoned: Lost along with Mars Polar Lander; no signal was ever received.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I carried no parachute, only a hardened ceramic nose cone. I was meant to strike the polar ice like a bullet, shattering the crust and driving my drill into the frozen layers beneath.
mars.howItWorked: Two-piece penetrator: aftbody stays at surface with antenna while forebody punches 1 meter deep on a flexible tether.
mars.scienceLegacy: Provided engineering data on ultra-high deceleration packaging (up to 30,000 g).
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: South polar ice impact site searched by HiRISE.
keyFacts: Named after famous Antarctic explorer Robert Falcon Scott.
Designed to survive impacts of up to 30,000 Gs.

mars.name: Deep Space 2 «Amundsen» Microprobe
mars.brief: The twin micro-penetrator meant to impact alongside Scott to test subsurface water-ice extraction with a miniature pyrotechnic laser.
mars.description: Named after Roald Amundsen, this identical penetrator entered the atmosphere ballistically but was never heard from again following the landing timeline.
mars.whyAbandoned: Loss on impact during ballistic descent.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I was Scott’s silent companion, diving into the southern ice cap with a micro-drill and battery. We sleep together in the layered polar terrain.
mars.howItWorked: Miniature tunable diode laser spectrometer designed to detect microscopic traces of water vapor in heated subsurface ice.
mars.scienceLegacy: Pioneered sub-miniature planetary instrument architectures.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Searched in Planum Australe by MRO HiRISE.
keyFacts: Named after Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen.
Equipped with tiny micro-heaters to vaporize sub-surface soil grains.

mars.name: Schiaparelli EDM Lander Impact Crater
mars.brief: The 2016 European test lander whose computer miscalculated its altitude as negative due to an IMU saturation glitch, cutting its rockets 3.7 km in the air.
mars.description: On October 19, 2016, the ExoMars Schiaparelli Entry, Descent, and Landing Demonstrator Module (EDM) was descending under its parachute when rapid oscillation saturated its Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) for just one second. The guidance computer computed a negative altitude, concluded it was already on the ground, cut the parachute, fired retrorockets for only 3 seconds, and plunged 3.7 km into Meridiani Planum at 540 km/h.
mars.whyAbandoned: Computer calculation error caused by 1-second IMU saturation during parachute turbulence.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: My parachute swung violently in the turbulent sky of Meridiani. For a single second, my rate sensor maxed out. My software panicked, calculated that I was already below ground, cut my parachute, and fired my rockets for three quick blinks before letting me plunge 3,700 meters into the red dirt.
mars.howItWorked: Equipped with DREAMS meteorological package, Doppler radar altimeter, and 9 hydrazine pulsed engines.
mars.scienceLegacy: The telemetry streamed during entry successfully validated ESA’s aerodynamic models, heat shield materials, and parachute deployment for the future Rosalind Franklin rover.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed by MRO HiRISE just days after impact, showing a prominent black impact crater 2.4 meters wide and a separate parachute white patch 1 km away.
keyFacts: Impacted at 540 km/h, leaving a distinct crater and dark blast swath.
Its parachute and heat shield were found resting cleanly 1.4 km from the crater.

mars.name: Viking 1 Heat Shield & Bioshield
mars.brief: The jettisoned 3.5-meter aeroshell and planetary bioshield cap that protected Viking 1 during hypersonic atmospheric entry.
mars.description: Separated at 6 km altitude before parachute release, impacting Chryse Planitia approximately 1.5 km from the Thomas Mutch station.
mars.whyAbandoned: Jettisoned during descent sequence.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I kept Viking 1 sterile and cold across nine months of interplanetary cruise, then absorbed the searing heat of Chryse Planitia entry.
mars.howItWorked: Phenolic-nylon ablator bonded to an aluminum honeycomb sub-structure.
mars.scienceLegacy: Validated planetary protection bioshield designs for Mars.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by MRO HiRISE west of the Viking 1 lander.
keyFacts: 3.5-meter diameter aeroshell.
First successful entry heat shield deployed on Mars.

mars.name: Viking 2 Discarded Heat Shield
mars.brief: Thermal heat shield of Viking 2 resting on the boulder-strewn volcanic plains of northern Utopia Planitia.
mars.description: Discarded pyrotechnically as planned at supersonic speed, impacting 2 km from the lander.
mars.whyAbandoned: Operational discard during entry.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I parted from Viking 2 in the high stratosphere of Utopia, letting its radar lock onto the volcanic fields below.
mars.howItWorked: Sacrificial thermal ablation.
mars.scienceLegacy: Demonstrated high-latitude entry aerodynamics.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Identified by HiRISE in Utopia Planitia.
keyFacts: Protected Viking 2 from 1,500°C friction heat.
Resting in the high northern plains of Utopia.

mars.name: Phoenix Heat Shield & Backshell Field
mars.brief: The parachute, backshell, and heat shield of the Phoenix lander lying in the arctic polygon plains.
mars.description: Separated during the terminal approach over Vastitas Borealis, photographed during descent by MRO HiRISE in mid-air.
mars.whyAbandoned: Planned separation during EDL.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: I was photographed by an orbiting satellite while I was still hanging in mid-air beneath my parachute, drifting down to the frozen northern tundra.
mars.howItWorked: Disk-gap-band parachute and ablative aeroshell.
mars.scienceLegacy: First time an incoming planetary lander was photographed in mid-flight by an orbital spacecraft.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Famously captured in mid-descent by MRO HiRISE on May 25, 2008.
keyFacts: Subject of the iconic «Phoenix suspended beneath parachute» orbital photo.

mars.name: Mars 3 Parachute & Heat Shield Site
mars.brief: The 11-meter conical parachute and heat shield identified by Russian space crowd-sourcers in 2013 on MRO HiRISE photos.
mars.description: In 2013, an online community of Russian space enthusiasts scouring MRO HiRISE images of Sirenum Terra discovered four distinct artifacts matching Mars 3's parachute, retrorocket motor, heat shield, and lander.
mars.whyAbandoned: Separated during Soviet 1971 entry.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: For forty-two years, I lay hidden in the dust of Sirenum Terra until citizen scientists on Earth spotted my bright white nylon canopy from satellite photos.
mars.howItWorked: Heavy-duty supersonic trailing parachute with central pull rocket.
mars.scienceLegacy: One of the most remarkable citizen-science visual recoveries in planetary history.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Found in 2013 by Vitaly Egorov and team on HiRISE image ESP_031024_1345.
keyFacts: Identified 42 years after landing by citizen space enthusiasts.
Verified by NASA JPL and HiRISE science teams.

mars.name: Zhurong Parachute & Backshell
mars.brief: The parachute and backshell that delivered China's Zhurong rover into Utopia Planitia, photographed by Zhurong itself while driving.
mars.description: In July 2021, Zhurong drove directly up to its jettisoned parachute and backshell, capturing stunning color panoramas of the crumpled white composite structure in the red dust.
mars.whyAbandoned: EDL hardware discarded before retrorocket touchdown.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: Zhurong drove across the sands of Utopia to visit me, rolling its camera mast within thirty meters of my crumpled white canopy to salute the shield that brought it down.
mars.howItWorked: Supersonic disk-gap-band parachute.
mars.scienceLegacy: Provided close-up engineering inspection of high-Mach Martian parachute deployment.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed both from the surface by Zhurong and from orbit by HiRISE and Tianwen-1.
keyFacts: Visited in-situ by the Zhurong rover on Sol 60.
Located 350 meters from the Tianwen-1 landing platform.

mars.name: Curiosity Tungsten Entry Balance Masses
mars.brief: Solid tungsten ballast weights ejected during guided entry to adjust the center-of-mass and provide aerodynamic lift.
mars.description: To fly MSL like a lifting glider through the Martian atmosphere, two 75 kg solid tungsten weights were pyrotechnically ejected minutes before parachute deployment.
mars.whyAbandoned: Center-of-mass shift maneuver during lifting entry.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: We are blocks of solid tungsten, dropped like stones into the desert so Curiosity could fly with aerodynamic lift through the upper sky of Mars.
mars.howItWorked: Mass offset ballast ejection creating controlled angle-of-attack lift.
mars.scienceLegacy: Pioneered guided lifting planetary entry, cutting landing ellipse size by 90%.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Identified on HiRISE imagery by impact craters with dark excavated subsoil.
keyFacts: Made of ultra-dense solid tungsten.
Allowed Curiosity to land within a tiny 20x7 km ellipse.

mars.name: Perseverance Tungsten Balance Weights
mars.brief: Solid ballast weights ejected during Range Trigger descent in Jezero Crater.
mars.description: Jettisoned at Mach 2 to realign the spacecraft for parachute deploy, impacting the plain outside the delta deposit.
mars.whyAbandoned: Trajectory trim ejection.
mars.firstPersonMonologue: We took the fall so Perseverance could trim its angle of attack and pop its parachute over Jezero Delta.
mars.howItWorked: Pyrotechnic rail ejection during guided atmospheric entry.
mars.scienceLegacy: Enabled Range Trigger parachute deployment precision.
mars.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by MRO HiRISE as two small crater dots.
keyFacts: Enriched with heavy tungsten alloy.
Part of the autonomous Entry, Descent, and Landing suite.

moon.name: Apollo 11 «Eagle» Descent Stage
moon.brief: The historic base of the lunar module Eagle, where Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin first set foot on another world on July 20, 1969.
moon.description: The descent stage served as the launch pad for the ascent stage that returned Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to orbit. Left behind at Tranquility Base with its golden Kapton thermal foil and four landing pads, it bears a commemorative plaque: «Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, July 1969 A.D. We came in peace for all mankind.»
moon.whyAbandoned: Designed as a permanent launch platform to remain at Tranquility Base.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was the perch from which human boots first touched another world. For half a century, the footprints of Armstrong and Aldrin have remained crisp in the gray dust around my gold-foil legs. In the airless stillness of the Sea of Tranquility, I stand as a testament that humanity can reach beyond its cradle.
moon.howItWorked: Used a throttleable bipropellant rocket engine (TRW LMDE) burning aerozine 50 and nitrogen tetroxide, allowing manual pilot throttling down to touchdown.
moon.scienceLegacy: Marked the dawn of human lunar surface exploration and returned 21.55 kg of pristine lunar rocks.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed in extraordinary detail by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LROC), showing the descent stage, astronaut footpaths, and the deployed EASEP package.
keyFacts: Touched down with only ~25 seconds of descent propellant remaining.
Bears a stainless-steel plaque signed by the Apollo 11 crew and President Richard Nixon.

moon.name: Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR)
moon.brief: An array of 100 quartz corner-cube prisms that requires zero power and is still used today by Earth observatories to measure the Moon’s distance to millimeter precision.
moon.description: Placed on the lunar surface by Buzz Aldrin, the Apollo 11 LRRR consists of 100 fused silica corner-cube prisms mounted in an aluminum tray. Whenever an observatory on Earth fires a high-powered pulsed laser at this spot, the corner cubes bounce photons directly back along their incoming path, allowing round-trip time-of-flight measurements.
moon.whyAbandoned: Designed to operate passively forever with zero internal batteries or electronics.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I need no batteries, no wires, no commands from Earth. For over fifty years, astronomers have aimed emerald lasers at my hundred quartz prisms. In 2.5 seconds, I bounce their light straight back into their telescopes, proving that the Moon is drifting away from Earth at 3.8 centimeters per year.
moon.howItWorked: Utilizes optical corner-cube retroreflection: three mutually perpendicular mirrors reflect incoming photons back in the exact opposite direction regardless of orientation.
moon.scienceLegacy: Proved the Moon is receding from Earth at 3.8 cm/year, verified Einstein’s general relativity equivalence principle, and confirmed the Moon possesses a fluid core.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Identified by LROC NAC 15 meters south of the Eagle descent stage.
keyFacts: The only Apollo 11 surface science instrument still in active scientific use today.
Measures the Earth-Moon distance (~384,400 km) with millimeter precision.

moon.name: Apollo 11 Passive Seismic Experiment (PSEP)
moon.brief: The first seismometer placed on another world, powered by solar arrays and radioisotope heaters.
moon.description: Deployed 16.8 meters from Eagle, PSEP recorded astronaut footsteps, venting from the lunar module, and natural micrometeorite impacts before overheating after 21 days.
moon.whyAbandoned: Solar-powered without battery backup; overheated during lunar noon and failed during its second lunar night.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I felt the heavy thud of Armstrong and Aldrin’s boots as they bounded across the regolith. For three weeks, my sensors recorded the quiet creaks of the Moon until the searing heat of lunar noon overwhelmed my circuits.
moon.howItWorked: Three long-period seismometers and one short-period vertical sensor measured micro-vibrations in the lunar crust.
moon.scienceLegacy: Proved that the lunar interior is seismically quiet compared to Earth and that seismic waves ring for hours in bone-dry rock.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by LROC as a distinct bright reflection east of the Eagle descent stage.
keyFacts: Recorded the astronaut footsteps as they walked on the lunar soil.
Used small radioisotope heater units (RHUs) containing Plutonium-238 to survive the freezing lunar night.

moon.name: Apollo 11 Eagle Ascent Stage Impact
moon.brief: The upper crew cabin of Eagle that lifted Armstrong and Aldrin off the surface and was later deorbited into the lunar plains.
moon.description: After docking with the command module Columbia in lunar orbit, Eagle was jettisoned. Its orbit decayed and it impacted the lunar surface at ~1.6 km/s.
moon.whyAbandoned: Jettisoned after transferring lunar samples and crew to Columbia.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I carried the first Moonwalkers back into the black sky to safety. My mission accomplished, Columbia cut me loose. I circled the gray craters until lunar gravity pulled me into a final dive into the mare.
moon.howItWorked: Fixed-thrust hypergolic ascent engine producing 15.6 kN of thrust with zero restart capability—it had to work on the first try.
moon.scienceLegacy: Demonstrated successful rendezvous and docking in lunar orbit.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Impact region photographed across Mare Tranquillitatis by LROC.
keyFacts: Carried 21.5 kg of priceless lunar samples into lunar orbit.
Impact velocity approximately 1.6 km/s (5,760 km/h).

moon.name: Apollo 12 «Intrepid» & ALSEP Station
moon.brief: The pinpoint landing module piloted by Pete Conrad to touch down just 160 meters from the robotic Surveyor 3 lander.
moon.description: Apollo 12 demonstrated precision landing by touching down within walking distance of the robotic Surveyor 3, which had landed 2.5 years earlier. Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked over, inspected Surveyor 3, and cut off its TV camera and mechanical scoop to bring back to Earth.
moon.whyAbandoned: Descent stage served as the launch platform for the ascent stage.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: They called my landing a pinpoint triumph. In the vast Ocean of Storms, I hovered and settled just 160 meters from a sleeping robot named Surveyor 3. Bean and Conrad walked between us like time travelers visiting an ancient predecessor.
moon.howItWorked: Advanced lunar guidance computer (LGC) landing radar algorithms enabled pinpoint touchdown within walking distance of a predetermined target.
moon.scienceLegacy: Deployed the first long-duration nuclear-powered ALSEP station and retrieved parts of Surveyor 3 to evaluate long-term space weathering.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by LROC with complete clarity, showing the Intrepid descent stage, Surveyor 3, the ALSEP station, and the dark paths walked by Conrad and Bean.
keyFacts: First pinpoint landing on another celestial body (landed 163 meters from Surveyor 3).
The crew recovered Surveyor 3's camera and mechanical arm to study how Earth equipment survives 31 months on the Moon.

moon.name: Apollo 12 ALSEP & SNAP-27 Nuclear Station
moon.brief: The first complete Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package, powered by a 73-watt plutonium RTG that ran for 8 consecutive years.
moon.description: Powered by a SNAP-27 Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator fueled by 3.8 kg of Plutonium-238, the Apollo 12 ALSEP operated continuously from 1969 until it was deliberately commanded off by NASA on September 30, 1977 due to budget constraints.
moon.whyAbandoned: Deactivated by NASA ground control in September 1977 for budgetary reasons after 8 years of flawless data transmission.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: With heat pulsing from my radioactive core, I sent 8 straight years of radio data back to Houston. When Apollo 13’s giant rocket stage smashed into the Moon, I felt the tremors and transmitted the famous discovery that the Moon rang like a bell.
moon.howItWorked: Plutonium-238 alpha decay heat generated 73.5 W of continuous electricity through lead-telluride thermocouples.
moon.scienceLegacy: Recorded thousands of deep moonquakes, solar wind ion fluxes, and lunar atmospheric gases.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed clearly by LROC west of the Intrepid descent stage.
keyFacts: Transmitted continuous scientific data to Earth for 8 consecutive years (1969–1977).
Recorded the seismic shockwaves of Apollo 13's Saturn V stage impact.

moon.name: Surveyor 3 (Visited by Apollo 12)
moon.brief: The robotic lander that touched down inside a crater in 1967 and was visited 31 months later by Apollo 12 astronauts.
moon.description: Surveyor 3 bounced twice upon landing when its radar sensors lost lock over high-reflectivity rocks. In November 1969, Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean hiked down into the crater, took photos, and removed its camera and surface sampler to return to Earth for forensic examination.
moon.whyAbandoned: Primary mission ended after its first lunar night in May 1967.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I thought I had been forgotten inside my crater. For two and a half years, I endured the searing days and frozen nights in solitude. Then, footsteps approached—two figures in white spacesuits with gold visors knelt beside me, unbolted my camera, and carried a piece of me home to Earth.
moon.howItWorked: Equipped with a pantograph robotic scoop arm that dug four trenches up to 18 cm deep, testing regolith bearing strength for the future Apollo lunar modules.
moon.scienceLegacy: Analysis of its retrieved parts on Earth revealed how microbes, optical lenses, and cables survive long-term radiation and thermal vacuum in deep space.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed inside Surveyor Crater by LROC, with the walking trail of Apollo 12 astronauts plainly visible.
keyFacts: The only robotic spacecraft on another world to ever be visited and examined in person by human beings.
Its retrieved TV camera is on permanent public display at the National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.

moon.name: Apollo 12 Intrepid Ascent Stage Impact
moon.brief: The upper stage of Intrepid, deliberately crashed into the Moon to calibrate the newly deployed Apollo 12 seismometer.
moon.description: After the crew rejoined the command module Yankee Clipper, ground controllers fired Intrepid’s ascent engine to drive it into the surface 72 km from the landing site. The impact released energy equivalent to one ton of TNT, producing a seismic signal that reverberated for over an hour.
moon.whyAbandoned: Intentionally crashed to perform the first active seismic sounding of the lunar interior.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: After sheltering Conrad and Bean on the surface and carrying them into orbit, I was given one final duty: sacrifice myself for science. I plunged into the plains at 1.68 km/s so my newly deployed seismometer could measure the shudder.
moon.howItWorked: Engine burn deorbited the spacecraft at a steep 15-degree angle directly toward the lunar regolith.
moon.scienceLegacy: Revealed that the lunar crust lacks water, causing seismic reverberations to ring continuously for over 60 minutes.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Impact crater identified by LROC with associated ejecta blanket.
keyFacts: Seismic waves from its impact lasted for over an hour, leading scientists to remark that the Moon «rang like a gong».
Impact energy equivalent to approximately 1 metric ton of TNT.

moon.name: Apollo 13 Saturn V S-IVB Impact Site
moon.brief: The giant 14-ton third stage of the Saturn V rocket, crashed into the Moon at 9,300 km/h with the kinetic energy of 11.5 tons of TNT.
moon.description: While the Apollo 13 crew fought for survival following an oxygen tank explosion on their spacecraft, ground controllers steered their massive S-IVB booster stage into the Moon. It slammed into Oceanus Procellarum at 2.58 km/s (9,288 km/h), creating a 30-meter crater. The seismic shockwave struck the Apollo 12 seismometer 137 km away, ringing for over 3 hours.
moon.whyAbandoned: Targeted for deliberate lunar impact to provide high-energy seismic data for the Apollo 12 ALSEP.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was the giant who propelled human beings toward the Moon. When they uncoupled from my nose, I was aimed straight at the lunar soil. Fourteen tons of aluminum and titanium struck the basalt at 2.58 kilometers per second. My explosion equaled eleven tons of TNT, sending shockwaves through the crust that vibrated for three hours.
moon.howItWorked: Used auxiliary propulsion system (APS) ullage thrusters to perform an orbital deflection maneuver straight into the Moon.
moon.scienceLegacy: Provided the first calibrated deep-crustal seismic soundings, demonstrating that the lunar crust is 60–70 km thick in that region.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed in high resolution by LROC, showing a distinct 30-meter impact crater with dark ejecta rays extending for hundreds of meters.
keyFacts: Weighed nearly 14 metric tons at impact—the heaviest manmade objects ever crashed on the Moon.
The seismic reverberation lasted for 3 hours and 20 minutes on the Apollo 12 seismometer.

moon.name: Apollo 14 «Antares» Descent Stage
moon.brief: The landing base from which Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell explored the rugged Fra Mauro highlands, and where Shepard hit two golf balls.
moon.description: Apollo 14 explored the geological ejecta blanket formed by the catastrophic Imbrium basin impact. The descent stage sits in the rolling hills of Fra Mauro, where Shepard famously pulled out a makeshift 6-iron golf club and struck two golf balls «miles and miles and miles».
moon.whyAbandoned: Permanent landing base structure.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I carried humanity to the highland hills of Fra Mauro after Apollo 13’s near-disaster. On my front porch, Alan Shepard swung a makeshift 6-iron club, sending two golf balls sailing across the airless vacuum into the cratered horizon.
moon.howItWorked: LM descent propulsion system with steerable gimbaled engine and laser altimeter radar.
moon.scienceLegacy: Returned 42.9 kg of lunar samples, dating the cataclysmic Imbrium impact basin to 3.85 billion years ago.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by LROC with clear tracks showing the crew’s walk to Cone Crater and back.
keyFacts: Site where Alan Shepard famously played golf on the Moon.
Crew reached the rim of the 300-meter Cone Crater during EVA 2.

moon.name: Apollo 14 Modular Equipment Transporter (MET)
moon.brief: The two-wheeled handcart pulled by Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell to haul geology tools and rock samples up Cone Crater.
moon.description: Nicknamed the «lunar rickshaw», the MET was a two-wheeled aluminum handcart equipped with nitrogen-filled rubber tires. While it carried heavy equipment, dragging it through the deep powdery regolith uphill proved exhausting for the astronauts, demonstrating the urgent need for a motorized rover.
moon.whyAbandoned: Left at Fra Mauro after sample collection.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was humanity’s first cart on another celestial body—a two-wheeled rickshaw with rubber tires. Mitchell and Shepard dragged me up the steep slopes of Cone Crater loaded with rocks and cameras until their breathing grew heavy.
moon.howItWorked: Lightweight aluminum tubular frame with specialized Michelin nitrogen-filled smooth rubber tires designed to avoid vacuum degradation.
moon.scienceLegacy: Direct operational feedback from the MET convinced NASA leadership to expedite development of the motorized Lunar Roving Vehicle for Apollo 15.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Located adjacent to the Apollo 14 ALSEP station in LROC imagery.
keyFacts: First wheeled transport vehicle ever pulled across the Moon.
Equipped with specially fabricated rubber tires filled with dry nitrogen.

moon.name: Apollo 14 Saturn V S-IVB Impact Site
moon.brief: Third stage of the Apollo 14 Saturn V, crashed at 2.54 km/s to test both Apollo 12 and newly deployed Apollo 14 seismometers.
moon.description: Impacted the Moon on February 4, 1971, releasing energy that allowed scientists to calibrate seismic wave velocity through the deep lunar mantle.
moon.whyAbandoned: Targeted seismic impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: Fourteen tons of rocket plunged into the lunar desert south of the Sea of Islands. My crash sent seismic echoes through both Apollo 12 and 14 stations simultaneously.
moon.howItWorked: Deflected into a collision trajectory via hypergolic propellant dump.
moon.scienceLegacy: Allowed cross-triangulation between multiple seismic stations to map lunar mantle density.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Identified by LROC with an asymmetrical 35-meter crater.
keyFacts: Impacted at 2.54 km/s (9,144 km/h).
Recorded simultaneously by two active ALSEP seismic stations.

moon.name: Apollo 15 «Falcon» Descent Stage
moon.brief: The first «J-mission» landing stage, engineered for extended 3-day stays and capable of carrying the first motorized lunar rover.
moon.description: Touching down between the towering 4,500-meter Apennine Mountains and the deep chasm of Hadley Rille, Falcon was the first upgraded extended-stay lunar module. David Scott and James Irwin lived on the Moon for 66.9 hours, conducting three EVAs.
moon.whyAbandoned: Permanent landing base.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I touched down in the shadows of the Apennine Mountains, whose peaks rise higher than the Alps into the black sky. In my cargo bay rested humanity’s first car for another world.
moon.howItWorked: Carried extra propellant tanks and life support consumables to double surface stay duration to 67 hours.
moon.scienceLegacy: Facilitated discovery of the famous «Genesis Rock» (anorthosite), dating back to the formation of the lunar primordial crust 4.1 billion years ago.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: High-resolution LROC images reveal the Falcon base, LRV tracks, and the rim of Hadley Rille.
keyFacts: First mission to deploy the Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV).
Crew collected the legendary 4-billion-year-old «Genesis Rock».

moon.name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV-001)
moon.statusLabel: First Car Driven on the Moon (1971)
moon.brief: The historic first motorized vehicle driven by humans on another celestial body, parked 100 meters east of Falcon so its TV camera could film liftoff.
moon.description: Designed by Boeing and GM Delco, LRV-001 transformed lunar exploration by allowing David Scott and James Irwin to cover 27.8 kilometers at speeds up to 12 km/h. Powered by two 36-volt silver-zinc potassium hydroxide batteries driving four independent 1/4-horsepower electric wheel motors, it carried astronauts to the edge of Hadley Rille canyon.
moon.whyAbandoned: Left parked 100 meters away from the LM Falcon so its remote-controlled television camera could broadcast the ascent stage launch to Earth.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was the first car driven on another world. With electric motors humming in my woven wire wheels, I bounced over the plains of Hadley, carrying Scott and Irwin along the edge of a canyon a kilometer wide. When their mission ended, they parked me facing Falcon, and my camera sent the picture of their liftoff to televisions across the Earth.
moon.howItWorked: Four 0.25-horsepower electric motors inside each wheel hub, with woven piano-wire mesh tires and titanium chevron treads for grip on loose dust.
moon.scienceLegacy: Expanded the human exploration radius from hundreds of meters on foot to over 27 kilometers, revolutionizing geological sampling.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: LROC NAC images clearly show the rover parked with its antenna deployed east of the Falcon descent stage.
keyFacts: Traveled a total distance of 27.76 km (17.25 miles).
Equipped with wire-mesh wheels made of zinc-coated steel piano wire.

moon.name: Apollo 15 LRRR-300 Retroreflector Array
moon.brief: The largest retroreflector array on the Moon, containing 300 corner-cube prisms that still return 75% of all laser ranging data back to Earth today.
moon.description: Three times larger than the arrays of Apollo 11 and 14, this 300-prism reflector provides the highest optical return signal of any retroreflector on the Moon, making it the primary target for laser ranging stations worldwide.
moon.whyAbandoned: Passive optical prism array operating without power.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: With three hundred fused quartz prisms, I am the brightest mirror on the Moon. For over half a century, laser pulses from France, Texas, and Germany have pinged my face every night, charting the subtle gravitational wobble of our satellite.
moon.howItWorked: Three hundred 3.8-cm diameter suprasil quartz corner-cube prisms mounted inside a hinged beryllium-alloy panel.
moon.scienceLegacy: Accounts for the vast majority of all lunar laser ranging scientific measurements taken from Earth over the last 50 years.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Visible in LROC imagery as an intensely reflective pixel signature near the Apollo 15 ALSEP.
keyFacts: Contains 300 corner-cube quartz prisms—three times larger than Apollo 11.
Generates 75% of all laser ranging measurements between Earth and the Moon.

moon.name: Apollo 15 Saturn V S-IVB Impact Site
moon.brief: Deliberate 14-ton rocket impact at 2.58 km/s recorded by seismometers at Apollo 12 and 14.
moon.description: Created a 32-meter impact crater, providing deep crustal seismic acoustic data.
moon.whyAbandoned: Seismic sounding mission.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I struck the plains at nine thousand kilometers per hour, sending shockwaves to the seismometers waiting hundreds of kilometers away.
moon.howItWorked: Targeted collision using propellant venting and APU burn.
moon.scienceLegacy: Confirmed structural seismic velocity discontinuities at 25 km and 60 km depth in the lunar crust.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by LROC with distinct radial ejecta patterns.
keyFacts: Weighed 14,036 kg at impact.
Crater diameter approximately 32 meters.

moon.name: Apollo 16 «Orion» Descent Stage
moon.brief: The lunar highland exploration station where John Young and Charlie Duke proved that the lunar highlands were impact breccias, not volcanic flows.
moon.description: Landing in the Descartes Highlands, Apollo 16 tested pre-mission theories that the bright lunar highlands were formed by volcanic action. Instead, Young and Duke discovered that nearly all rocks were impact breccias formed by catastrophic asteroid bombardments.
moon.whyAbandoned: Permanent landing base.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I brought Young and Duke to the bright Descartes plateau. Geologists thought they would find volcanic lavas here; instead, our samples revealed that the highlands were shattered by billions of years of asteroid impacts.
moon.howItWorked: Highland landing radar and steerable bipropellant descent engine.
moon.scienceLegacy: Radically overturned lunar geological models, proving the ancient origin of the lunar crust as anorthositic impact breccias.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by LROC with rover tracks leading up Stone Mountain.
keyFacts: Collected 95.8 kg of lunar highland rocks, including the massive 11.7 kg «Big Muley» rock.
Disproved the theory of lunar highland volcanism.

moon.name: Apollo 16 Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV-002)
moon.brief: The rover famous for the «Lunar Grand Prix», where John Young executed high-speed 180-degree power-slides on film.
moon.description: Covered 26.6 kilometers across Descartes Highlands, climbing up the 20-degree slopes of Stone Mountain and driving to the rim of the 1-kilometer-wide North Ray Crater.
moon.whyAbandoned: Parked to record Orion ascent.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: Young took me out on a flat stretch of Descartes regolith and showed the world what a lunar car could do—sliding, fishtailing, and kicking up rooster tails of dust in one-sixth gravity.
moon.howItWorked: Four 1/4-horsepower DC electric motors and dual Ackerman steering systems.
moon.scienceLegacy: Demonstrated mobility on steep highland slopes.
