moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed parked north of the Orion descent stage by LROC.
keyFacts: John Young set an off-world lunar speed record of 18.0 km/h (11.2 mph).
Traveled 26.55 km across three EVAs.

moon.name: Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera / Spectrograph
moon.brief: The first astronomical telescope placed on the Moon, photographing the Earth’s geocorona and deep-space nebulae in ultraviolet light.
moon.description: Designed by Dr. George Carruthers, this 3-inch Schmidt electronographic camera was set up in the shadow of the lunar module to photograph Earth, stars, and the Large Magellanic Cloud in far-ultraviolet wavelengths blocked by Earth's atmosphere.
moon.whyAbandoned: Placed on surface; film cartridge retrieved by John Young.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was the first telescope erected on the Moon. Looking back at Earth in far-ultraviolet light, I captured the luminous halo of hydrogen gas enveloping the planet.
moon.howItWorked: Used potassium bromide photocathodes and electron optics to record 50-200 nanometer ultraviolet photons directly onto film.
moon.scienceLegacy: Provided the first ultraviolet images of the Earth’s geocorona and interstellar hydrogen clouds from an off-world platform.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by LROC in the shadow zone of the LM Orion.
keyFacts: First astronomical observatory operated on another planetary body.
Invented by African-American astrophysicist and inventor Dr. George Carruthers.

moon.name: Apollo 17 «Challenger» Descent Stage
moon.brief: The final manned landing site of the 20th century, where Gene Cernan and geologist Harrison Schmitt spent 75 hours on the surface.
moon.description: Apollo 17 was the grand scientific climax of the Apollo program. Gene Cernan and professional geologist Dr. Harrison «Jack» Schmitt lived in the breathtaking Taurus-Littrow valley for over three days, exploring towering massifs and finding volcanic orange glass beads.
moon.whyAbandoned: Permanent landing base.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was the final home for Apollo astronauts. In Taurus-Littrow, where mountains climb higher than the Grand Canyon walls, Gene Cernan stepped back into my hatch and spoke of returning with peace and hope for all mankind. For over fifty years, no human has been back.
moon.howItWorked: Heaviest LM configuration with maximized payload, carrying 110.5 kg of geological samples back into orbit.
moon.scienceLegacy: Discovery of 3.64-billion-year-old orange volcanic glass beads in Shorty Crater proved explosive pyroclastic volcanism in lunar history.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: LROC NAC images show the Challenger descent stage with footpaths leading to the ALSEP and the parked rover.
keyFacts: The last place on the Moon touched by human boots (Eugene Cernan on December 14, 1972).
Returned 110.5 kg of lunar samples—the largest haul of any Apollo mission.

moon.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV-003)
moon.brief: The final lunar rover, famous for the emergency improvised repair of its broken fender using taped lunar maps and clamps.
moon.description: Covered a record-breaking 35.89 km across Taurus-Littrow. During EVA 1, Gene Cernan’s hammer caught the rear fiberglass fender, tearing it off and raining blinding dust over the rover. That night, astronauts taped four laminated heavy-paper lunar maps together with gray duct tape and clamped them on, creating a legendary improvised field repair.
moon.whyAbandoned: Parked at «VIP site» 150m east of Challenger to broadcast liftoff.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: They broke my fender on our first drive, and the dust blinded our navigation. But human ingenuity patched me: four plastic maps and a strip of gray duct tape held fast for thirty kilometers across the valley. I am still parked here, looking out toward the South Massif.
moon.howItWorked: Wired with an integrated directional gyro navigation computer and odometry processor.
moon.scienceLegacy: Traveled to Shorty Crater, Camelot Crater, and the North Massif, maximizing scientific collection.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed clearly by LROC at the VIP site east of Challenger.
keyFacts: Holds the record for the longest total distance driven on the Moon by humans: 35.89 km (22.3 miles).
Its improvised map-and-duct-tape fender became one of NASA's most celebrated field hacks.

moon.name: Apollo 17 Traverse Gravimeter & ALSEP
moon.brief: A vibrating-string accelerometer mounted on the LRV that measured local gravity at 26 stops across the Taurus-Littrow valley.
moon.description: Measured subtle changes in local gravitational acceleration to map the thickness of the dense basaltic lava layer filling the valley floor.
moon.whyAbandoned: Survey experiment completed.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: At every stop of the rover, I weighed the hidden crust beneath our wheels. My measurements revealed that a river of ancient basaltic lava over a kilometer deep fills the floor of Taurus-Littrow.
moon.howItWorked: Used a precision vibrating reed suspended between magnets to measure variations of 1 milligal in surface gravity.
moon.scienceLegacy: Mapped the first high-resolution cross-section of a lunar mountain valley.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Identified in the Apollo 17 ALSEP array by LROC.
keyFacts: Conducted gravity surveys at 26 different stops along the rover route.
Determined that the basalt valley floor is 1.4 km thick.

moon.name: Luna 2 Impact Site
moon.statusLabel: First Human Artifact on the Moon (1959)
moon.brief: The first human-made object in history to ever reach the surface of another celestial body, impacting on September 14, 1959.
moon.description: On September 14, 1959, Luna 2 achieved the first artificial impact on the Moon. Traveling at 3.3 km/s, it scattered commemorative titanium pentagonal pennants engraved with the Soviet hammer and sickle and the date «СССР СЕНТЯБРЬ 1959».
moon.whyAbandoned: Direct high-velocity ballistic impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was the first metal from Earth to touch the Moon. When I struck the Marsh of Decay at three kilometers per second, I vaporized into dust, scattering tiny steel emblems across the gray desert to announce that humanity had crossed the threshold of worlds.
moon.howItWorked: Spherical pressurized spacecraft equipped with magnetometers and scintillation counters that sent radio signals until the microsecond of impact.
moon.scienceLegacy: Discovered that the Moon has no significant global magnetic field or radiation belts comparable to Earth’s Van Allen belts.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Crater region verified in Palus Putredinis by LROC cartographic studies.
keyFacts: First artificial object to reach another celestial body in human history.
Carried two explosive sphere pennants with 144 pentagonal stainless-steel medallions.

moon.name: Luna 9 Lander
moon.brief: The historic spherical lander that achieved the first survivable soft landing on the Moon, proving the ground was solid and would not swallow landers.
moon.description: Before Luna 9, some astronomers feared the lunar surface was covered in a deep sea of powdery dust that would swallow any arriving spacecraft. Ejected from its descent stage, the 100 kg capsule inflated an airbag, bounced to a stop, bloomed open four petal shields, and transmitted the first panoramic photos from the surface.
moon.whyAbandoned: Battery depleted after 3 days of historic photographic transmissions.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: They feared the Moon was an ocean of quicksand that would swallow ships whole. I was dropped inside an airbag, rolled to a stop, and popped open my four petals. I proved the ground was solid stone and sent back humanity’s first photograph from the surface of an alien world.
moon.howItWorked: Used a KTDU-5A retrorocket engine triggered by a 5-meter mechanical ground-probe rod, popping out a 58 cm spherical payload in an airbag.
moon.scienceLegacy: Proved the lunar regolith can support the weight of landers and astronauts, removing the greatest psychological fear of the Apollo program.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Identified by LROC NAC in Oceanus Procellarum.
keyFacts: First spacecraft to make a soft touchdown and transmit images from the lunar surface.
Transmitted four panoramic image sequences before its batteries expired.

moon.name: Luna 13 Lander
moon.brief: The 1966 lander equipped with an explosive penetrometer that directly hammered into the regolith to measure soil density.
moon.description: Soft-landed on Christmas Eve 1966, Luna 13 deployed two mechanical booms carrying an explosive penetrometer and a gamma-ray radiation densitometer.
moon.whyAbandoned: Chemical battery exhaustion.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I fired a miniature rocket penetrometer straight down into the lunar dust, testing its hardness for the future Soviet and Apollo explorers.
moon.howItWorked: Pyrotechnic penetrometer driven into the surface by a solid rocket charge.
moon.scienceLegacy: Calculated regolith mechanical bearing capacity down to 30 cm.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by LROC in western Oceanus Procellarum.
keyFacts: Carried an explosive-driven mechanical soil penetrometer.
Returned 5 complete panoramas of the lunar surface.

moon.name: Luna 15 Crash Site
moon.brief: The Soviet robotic sample-return probe that crashed into Mare Crisium while Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were walking on the Moon.
moon.description: In an extraordinary climax to the Space Race, Luna 15 was launched just three days before Apollo 11 in a desperate attempt to scoop up lunar soil and return it to Moscow before Apollo returned. On July 21, 1969, while Armstrong and Aldrin were still on the Moon, Luna 15 fired its deorbit burn, lost radar lock, and slammed into the side of a mountain at 480 km/h.
moon.whyAbandoned: High-speed impact crash during terminal descent.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I raced across the cosmos to beat Apollo 11. While Armstrong and Aldrin stood in the Sea of Tranquility, I dove toward the Sea of Crises. But the mountains rose too fast, and I crashed into a hillside just hours before they lifted off for home.
moon.howItWorked: Automated sample-return spacecraft with a robotic core drill and spherical Earth-return rocket capsule.
moon.scienceLegacy: Led to historic real-time communications between the US and USSR to ensure Luna 15’s telemetry would not interfere with Apollo 11.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Impact crater identified in Mare Crisium on LROC imagery.
keyFacts: Crashed into the Moon at the exact same moment Armstrong and Aldrin were preparing for liftoff.
Prompted the first emergency direct telecommunication channel between NASA and the Soviet Academy of Sciences.

moon.name: Luna 16 Descent Stage
moon.brief: The historic lander that executed the first fully robotic sample return in human history, drilling 35 cm into Mare Fecunditatis.
moon.description: On September 20, 1970, Luna 16 executed an automated night landing in Mare Fecunditatis. A rotary drill bored 35 cm into the soil, extracted 101 grams of regolith, and sealed it into an ascent rocket that launched back to Earth without a human aboard.
moon.whyAbandoned: Descent stage remained as launch pad.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: Without human eyes or hands, I landed in the dark of Mare Fecunditatis, drilled deep into the frozen dust, and packed a capsule of soil into my rocket. I fired my ascent engine toward the stars, sending the first robotic lunar sample back to Earth.
moon.howItWorked: Autonomous hollow drill arm with mechanical transfer mechanism into a spherical heat-shield capsule.
moon.scienceLegacy: Proved robotic sample return was possible at a fraction of the cost of manned flights, returning 101 grams of lunar basalt.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by LROC in Mare Fecunditatis.
keyFacts: First automated robotic sample return mission in space exploration history.
Its 101-gram soil sample was shared with scientists worldwide.

moon.name: Luna 17 & Lunokhod 1 Rover
moon.statusLabel: First Robotic Rover on Another World (1970)
moon.brief: The tub-shaped eight-wheeled giant that became the first remote-controlled robotic rover on another world, driving 10.5 km across Mare Imbrium.
moon.description: Resembling a bathtub on wheels with a convex solar lid, Lunokhod 1 rolled down Luna 17’s ramps on November 17, 1970. Driven by a five-man crew in Moscow using joysticks and delayed TV feeds, it traversed 10.5 km, analyzed regolith at 500 locations, and transmitted 20,000 television images.
moon.whyAbandoned: Its polonium-210 radioisotope heater decayed after 11 months, allowing its electronics to freeze during the lunar night.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was the first robotic rover to leave tracks on another world. With eight mesh wheels, I rolled across the Sea of Rains, steered by drivers in Moscow listening to the crackle of radio delay. For eleven months, I explored craters and hills, until the cold of the lunar night finally quieted my gears.
moon.howItWorked: Eight wire-mesh motorized wheels with independent suspension; heated at night by a Polonium-210 isotope heater and closed insulated lid.
moon.scienceLegacy: Carried a French corner-cube laser reflector, and in 2010—forty years after it went silent—astronomers at UCSD bounced a laser off Lunokhod 1, measuring its location to within a single centimeter.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Rediscovered in March 2010 by LROC NAC imagery, showing its wheel tracks and exact parking spot.
keyFacts: First remote-controlled mobile rover on any celestial body.
Driven by a five-person team in Simferopol/Moscow using low-frame-rate television cameras.

moon.name: Luna 21 & Lunokhod 2 Rover
moon.brief: The rover that held the off-world driving distance record of 39 km for over 40 years until passed by Opportunity on Mars.
moon.description: Lunokhod 2 landed inside Le Monnier crater on January 15, 1973. Featuring higher-frame-rate cameras and improved steering, it raced 39 kilometers in under four months across treacherous basalt rilles.
moon.whyAbandoned: On May 9, 1973, it drove into a steep crater. Its open solar lid scraped the rim, scooping up lunar dust. When the lid was closed for the night, the dust dumped directly onto the radiator panels, causing fatal overheating when the sun rose.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: For forty years, I held the crown for the longest journey driven on any world outside Earth. I crossed 39 kilometers of Le Monnier crater until my solar lid brushed a crater wall. When I shut my lid, the dust fell upon my radiators, and the heat of the sun overwhelmed me.
moon.howItWorked: Improved higher-rate scanning TV camera and advanced wheel odometry penetrometer.
moon.scienceLegacy: Mapped transition zone magnetism between mare basins and highland plateaus.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by LROC in Le Monnier crater along with its full 39 km wheel trail.
keyFacts: Held the planetary roving record of 39 km for 41 years until 2014.
Transmitted 86 panoramic sequences and over 80,000 television frames.

moon.name: Luna 24 Descent Stage
moon.brief: The last spacecraft to soft-land on the Moon for 37 years (until China’s Chang’e 3 in 2013), extracting a 2-meter deep core sample.
moon.description: Touching down in Mare Crisium, Luna 24 used an advanced rotary percussion drill with a flexible helical tube to extract an intact 2-meter core sample of the lunar subsoil (170 grams), proving the presence of trace water molecules in lunar regolith decades before it was officially accepted.
moon.whyAbandoned: Descent stage left as launch platform.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was the last visitor to touch the Moon for nearly four decades. I drilled two meters into Mare Crisium and sent my sample capsule home. Then a deep silence fell over the Moon that lasted thirty-seven years.
moon.howItWorked: Advanced rotary percussive core drill with internal flexible spiral tape to preserve stratigraphy.
moon.scienceLegacy: Soviet scientists published in 1978 that Luna 24’s sample contained 0.1% water by mass, an early clue to lunar water ice that was initially dismissed in the West.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed in Mare Crisium by LROC.
keyFacts: Final Soviet spacecraft to touch the Moon.
The last lunar soft landing until China's Chang'e 3 arrived 37 years later in 2013.

moon.name: Lunar Prospector (Shoemaker Burial Impact)
moon.brief: The spacecraft that mapped lunar water ice from orbit and carried the cremated ashes of legendary planetary geologist Eugene Shoemaker to his final rest on the Moon.
moon.description: Carrying a brass capsule with the ashes of pioneering geologist Eugene Shoemaker (co-discoverer of Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 who trained the Apollo astronauts), Lunar Prospector completed its orbital mission and was deliberately crashed at 1.7 km/s into a permanently shadowed crater at the south pole.
moon.whyAbandoned: Controlled deorbit impact into permanently shadowed south polar crater to test for water ice plume.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I carry humanity’s only off-world burial. Inside my body rests a brass capsule with the ashes of Eugene Shoemaker, wrapped in an inscription of Romeo and Juliet. I dove into a permanently shadowed crater at the south pole, where his resting place will never see the sun.
moon.howItWorked: Spin-stabilized probe with gamma-ray and neutron spectrometers.
moon.scienceLegacy: Discovered high concentrations of hydrogen in the lunar polar craters, proving the existence of subsurface water ice.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Shoemaker Crater south pole rim mapped by LROC and LOLA.
keyFacts: Eugene Shoemaker remains the only human being whose ashes are buried on the Moon.
The brass foil was engraved with images of Comet Hale-Bopp and Meteor Crater.

moon.name: LCROSS Centaur Upper Stage Impact
moon.brief: The 2.2-ton rocket stage that smashed into Cabeus crater at 9,000 km/h, excavating a massive debris plume that proved the Moon holds billions of gallons of water ice.
moon.description: On October 9, 2009, the spent Centaur rocket upper stage slammed into the pitch-black floor of Cabeus crater at 2.5 km/s. The kinetic impact vaporized deep permafrost, throwing up a 10-kilometer-high plume of soil and gas containing over 155 kg of pure water ice, hydroxyl, methane, and ammonia.
moon.whyAbandoned: Targeted kinetic impactor for plume spectroscopy.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I struck the darkest place in the solar system—a crater floor that has not seen sunlight for two billion years. My crash blasted 300 tons of ancient ice into the sunlight, confirming that the Moon holds the water humanity needs to journey to Mars.
moon.howItWorked: Kinetic energy excavation creating a 20-meter crater and vaporizing volatile compounds for real-time spectroscopy.
moon.scienceLegacy: Provided conclusive spectroscopic proof of water ice on the Moon, transforming human plans for future permanent lunar bases.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Impact crater thermal glow detected by LRO DIVINER instrument.
keyFacts: Excavated an estimated 155 kg (342 lbs) of water vapor from the permanently shadowed crater floor.
Impact velocity of 2.5 km/s (9,000 km/h).

moon.name: Chang'e 3 Lander & «Yutu-1» Rover
moon.brief: The mission that ended the 37-year dry spell of lunar landings, deploying the «Jade Rabbit» rover to explore young volcanic basalts.
moon.description: Touched down in northern Mare Imbrium on December 14, 2013. The lander operated the first robotic lunar ultraviolet telescope, while the 140 kg Yutu rover drove across the plains analyzing volcanic rocks before a mechanical control fault immobilized it on Sol 2.
moon.whyAbandoned: Rover immobilized by electrical cable snag on rocks; continued transmitting as a stationary station for 31 months.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: Thirty-seven years after Luna 24, I brought humanity’s robotic eyes back to the lunar soil. In the Sea of Rains, my gold solar panels opened, and Yutu rolled into the dust.
moon.howItWorked: Variable-thrust 7,500 N engine with laser 3D terrain hazard avoidance.
moon.scienceLegacy: Discovered a new type of basalt rich in ilmenite and titanium, shedding light on late-stage lunar volcanism.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed in Mare Imbrium by LROC NAC.
keyFacts: First spacecraft to make a soft touchdown on the Moon in the 21st century.
Operated an active Moon-based ultraviolet astronomy telescope.

moon.name: Chang'e 4 Lander & «Yutu-2» Rover (Far Side)
moon.statusLabel: First Landing on the Far Side of the Moon
moon.locationName: Von Kármán Crater, South Pole-Aitken Basin
moon.brief: The historic first mission ever to land on the mysterious Far Side of the Moon, communicating via the Queqiao relay satellite in halo orbit.
moon.description: On January 3, 2019, Chang'e 4 made history by executing the first soft landing on the lunar Far Side inside Von Kármán crater within the ancient South Pole-Aitken basin. Because the Moon’s body blocks direct line-of-sight to Earth, signals are relayed via the Queqiao satellite stationed at the Earth-Moon L2 Lagrange point.
moon.whyAbandoned: Still operational on the far side; intermittently dormant during freezing 14-day lunar nights.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I stand where Earth never shines in the sky. Behind the shielded curvature of the Moon, sheltered from all the noisy radio broadcasts of human civilization, I look out upon the ancient craters of the Far Side, whispering my findings to a satellite hovering in the black beyond.
moon.howItWorked: Communicates through the Queqiao relay satellite orbiting the L2 Lagrange point 65,000 km beyond the Moon.
moon.scienceLegacy: Proved the composition of the deep lunar mantle exposed by the giant South Pole-Aitken impact basin.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged on the floor of Von Kármán crater by NASA’s LROC.
keyFacts: First and only human mission to land on the Far Side of the Moon.
Carried a biosphere experiment that sprouted the first plant seeds (cotton) on another world.

moon.name: Chandrayaan-3 «Vikram» & «Pragyan»
moon.brief: India’s historic landing near the lunar south pole, deploying the Pragyan rover to confirm the presence of sulfur in the polar soil.
moon.description: On August 23, 2023, India became the fourth nation to land on the Moon and the first ever to land in the rugged south polar region. The Vikram lander touched down at Shiv Shakti Point, deployed the Pragyan rover, measured soil temperatures down to 8 cm depth (ChaSTE), and verified elemental sulfur with Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS).
moon.whyAbandoned: Designed for a 1-lunar-day (14 Earth days) mission; entered planned sleep before the -180°C south polar night without radioisotope heaters.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: At Shiv Shakti Point, where the shadows stretch long and sharp across the craters of the south, I unfurled my ramp for Pragyan. For two weeks in the polar sun, we confirmed that sulfur and metals sleep in the permafrost, before the freezing polar dark enveloped our antennas.
moon.howItWorked: Laser Doppler velocimeter and four 800 N throttleable liquid engines with real-time hazard avoidance computer vision.
moon.scienceLegacy: First in-situ temperature gradient measurements of polar regolith and definitive confirmation of sulfur on the lunar surface.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed by both NASA’s LROC and ISRO’s Chandrayaan-2 Orbiter camera with centimeter resolution.
keyFacts: Made India the first nation in history to land near the lunar south pole.
The landing site was officially named «Shiv Shakti Point» by the IAU.

moon.name: SLIM (Smart Lander) & Sora-Q Rovers
moon.brief: Japan’s «Moon Sniper» that achieved pinpoint landing within 3 meters of its target on a 15-degree crater slope, deploying the Sora-Q transformable ball rover.
moon.description: Nicknamed the «Moon Sniper», SLIM demonstrated vision-based autonomous navigation by landing just 3 to 4 meters away from its target point on the steep slope of Shioli crater. Although an engine nozzle detached during the final seconds causing it to land nose-down, it survived three brutal lunar nights and its palm-sized transformable ball rover (LEV-2 / Sora-Q) took a world-famous photo of the inverted lander.
moon.whyAbandoned: Mission completed after surviving three unexpected lunar nights without heaters.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: They called me the Moon Sniper. I aimed for a 3-meter bullseye on the steep wall of Shioli crater and hit it. Even though I tumbled forward onto my head, my tiny robot companion rolled out like a toy ball, snapped my picture, and sent it to Earth.
moon.howItWorked: Real-time Crater Matching autonomous navigation comparing descent photos against onboard satellite maps in milliseconds.
moon.scienceLegacy: Transformed planetary landing technology from «landing where we can» to «landing exactly where we want».
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed on the slope of Shioli crater by LROC.
keyFacts: Achieved the most accurate pinpoint landing in history (within 3 to 4 meters of target).
Deployed Sora-Q, a baseball-sized transformable rover co-developed with toy company Takara Tomy.

moon.name: Chang'e 6 Descent Stage (Far Side)
moon.brief: The 2024 descent stage that executed the historic first-ever sample return from the Far Side of the Moon, returning 1,935 grams of ancient mantle material.
moon.description: On June 1, 2024, Chang'e 6 landed inside the immense Apollo impact basin on the lunar Far Side. It drilled and scooped nearly 2 kilograms of pristine regolith, unveiled a miniature national flag made of basalt fiber, and launched its ascent stage to dock in orbit and bring the samples back to Earth on June 25, 2024.
moon.whyAbandoned: Permanent landing base left in Apollo basin.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I dug into the oldest and deepest scar on the Moon: the South Pole-Aitken basin on the Far Side. With mechanical scoop and drill, I gathered two kilograms of rocks that had never seen the light of Earth, then watched my ascent stage carry them into orbit.
moon.howItWorked: High-speed autonomous drilling and scooping with basalt-fiber thermal insulation.
moon.scienceLegacy: Brought back humanity’s first physical samples from the Far Side of the Moon, revealing fundamental differences between the near and far side volcanic history.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged in the Apollo crater basin by LROC.
keyFacts: First mission in human history to return soil samples from the Far Side of the Moon.
Returned 1,935.3 grams of pristine lunar Far-Side material on June 25, 2024.

moon.name: Surveyor 1
moon.brief: The first American spacecraft to soft-land on the Moon, proving that the lunar surface could support the weight of the Apollo Lunar Module.
moon.description: Landing on June 2, 1966, inside a 100-kilometer ghost crater ring near Flamsteed in Oceanus Procellarum, Surveyor 1 returned 11,238 high-resolution television pictures, dispelling the theory that landers would sink into deep powdery dust.
moon.whyAbandoned: Batteries depleted after multiple lunar night survivals in August 1966.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was America’s first gentle touch upon the Moon. When my three footpads settled into Flamsteed Crater, my landing gear sunk only a few centimeters into the sand. I broadcast over eleven thousand photos back to Earth, telling Apollo that the ground was ready.
moon.howItWorked: Three throttleable vernier rocket engines and a solid-propellant main retro motor guided by Doppler radar altimetry.
moon.scienceLegacy: Directly validated the landing dynamics and pad footings used on the Apollo Lunar Module.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed in high resolution by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LROC) in 2009.
keyFacts: First American spacecraft to execute a soft touchdown on another world.
Transmitted 11,238 television frames before battery failure.

moon.name: Surveyor 2 Crash Site
moon.brief: Crashed into the Moon after one of its three vernier rocket engines failed to ignite during a mid-course correction burn.
moon.description: During a mid-course velocity adjustment, vernier engine number 3 failed to ignite, sending the spacecraft into an uncontrolled tumble at 136 RPM. Controllers fired retro-rockets in an attempt to stabilize, but the craft impacted Sinus Medii at high speed.
moon.whyAbandoned: Loss of control during midcourse flight.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: A single valve refused to open, and the sky began to spin. T tumbling at two revolutions per second, I plunged into Sinus Medii at full velocity, sacrificing myself to teach engineers how to make future Surveyors resilient.
moon.howItWorked: Vernier engine failure led to loss of triaxial attitude stabilization.
moon.scienceLegacy: Led to redesigned valve heater jackets and redundant ignition commands on Surveyors 3 through 7.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Impact crater zone identified near Copernicus crater in Sinus Medii.
keyFacts: Impact velocity of 2.6 km/s (9,360 km/h).
Engineers corrected the ignition anomaly on all subsequent Surveyor flights.

moon.name: Surveyor 4 Impact Site
moon.brief: Telemetry ceased abruptly 2.5 minutes before scheduled touchdown, likely due to an explosion of its solid-propellant retrorocket.
moon.description: Surveyor 4 executed a flawless flight until the final retro-rocket burn at an altitude of 47 kilometers. At T-minus 2.5 minutes to touchdown, all radio signals abruptly stopped.
moon.whyAbandoned: Catastrophic retrorocket explosion during final descent deceleration.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was minutes away from landing in the exact center of the Moon’s visible face. My retromotor was firing true until a sudden blast tore my transmitters apart in mid-air.
moon.howItWorked: Main retrorocket burn anomaly.
moon.scienceLegacy: Improved casing insulation on subsequent Surveyor retrorockets.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Sinus Medii impact crater field surveyed by LROC.
keyFacts: Signal was lost with just 2.5 minutes remaining until touchdown.
Impacted within the planned landing ellipse in Sinus Medii.

moon.name: Surveyor 5
moon.brief: Survived a critical helium leak in flight to soft-land in Mare Tranquillitatis, using an alpha-scattering instrument to discover lunar basalt.
moon.description: Despite losing helium pressure en route, ingenious ground reprogramming allowed Surveyor 5 to land safely on a 20-degree slope inside a small rimless crater in Mare Tranquillitatis. Its alpha-scattering spectrometer provided humanity’s first in-situ chemical analysis of lunar soil, proving the maria are composed of basaltic lava.
moon.whyAbandoned: Mission completed after surviving four lunar nights in December 1967.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: My tanks were bleeding helium, but Houston rewritten my descent equations in the dark of space. I landed on the slope of a crater in Mare Tranquillitatis, lowered my alpha spectrometer, and told humanity that the dark plains of the Moon were made of volcanic basalt.
moon.howItWorked: Curium-242 radioactive source bounced alpha particles off lunar soil atoms to calculate chemical element abundances via backscattering.
moon.scienceLegacy: Provided the first conclusive evidence that the lunar maria are volcanic basalt lavas rich in titanium and iron.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: LROC NAC images reveal Surveyor 5 resting inside its small crater.
keyFacts: Conducted the first off-world in-situ chemical analysis of extraterrestrial soil.
Returned 19,049 television frames to Earth.

moon.name: Surveyor 6
moon.brief: The first spacecraft in human history to launch off the surface of the Moon, firing its engines for 2.5 seconds to hop 2.4 meters.
moon.description: On November 17, 1967, one week after landing in Sinus Medii, NASA controllers fired Surveyor 6’s three vernier engines for 2.5 seconds. The lander lifted 3 meters off the surface, moved 2.4 meters sideways, and landed softly again, proving that rockets could reignite and take off from the lunar soil.
moon.whyAbandoned: Battery degradation during second lunar night in December 1967.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I landed once, and then I did what no machine had ever done: I fired my rockets from the lunar dust, leaped into the black sky, and landed again eight feet away. I proved that humanity could leave the Moon and fly back home.
moon.howItWorked: Liquid-fueled vernier rocket restart on the lunar surface.
moon.scienceLegacy: Demonstrated lunar liftoff physics, engine blast trenching, and soil erosion dynamics for the Apollo Ascent Stage.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by LROC in Sinus Medii, with both the original landing imprint and second touchdown pads visible.
keyFacts: First powered liftoff and flight from the surface of another celestial body.
Transmitted nearly 30,000 images back to Earth.

moon.name: Surveyor 7
moon.brief: The only Surveyor sent to the rugged southern highlands, touching down on the rocky ejecta blanket of Tycho crater.
moon.description: Unlike previous Surveyors aimed at smooth Apollo landing mare, Surveyor 7 was targeted to pure science on the rim of the spectacular Tycho impact crater. It detected green argon laser pulses beamed to it from Kitt Peak and Table Mountain observatories on Earth.
moon.whyAbandoned: Completed primary science operations; battery froze in February 1968.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was sent not for Apollo’s runways, but for pure wonder: the jagged, boulder-strewn rim of Tycho. Looking back at Earth, my camera photographed two tiny green pinpricks of light—laser beams fired at me by astronomers on California mountaintops.
moon.howItWorked: Equipped with both an alpha-scattering spectrometer and a surface sampler arm, which was used to push down an unseated alpha-scattering sensor head.
moon.scienceLegacy: Demonstrated that highland rocks contain far less iron and titanium than the dark volcanic maria, supporting the lunar magma ocean theory.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed by LROC on the rugged ejecta blanket north of Tycho crater.
keyFacts: First spacecraft to detect optical laser beams transmitted from the surface of the Earth.
Only Surveyor mission sent to an unexplored highland region.

moon.name: Ranger 4 Crash Site
moon.statusLabel: First US Craft on the Moon (1962)
moon.brief: The first American spacecraft to reach the surface of the Moon, crashing onto the Far Side after a master clock failure.
moon.description: Launched on April 23, 1962, a power failure in its central computer and sequencer froze its telemetry and solar panel deployment. It tracked ballistically and crashed onto the lunar Far Side at 9,600 km/h on April 26, 1962.
moon.whyAbandoned: Ballistic impact crash.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: My clock failed in deep space, blinding my cameras. But my trajectory was true: I crossed the void and struck the Far Side of the Moon, becoming America’s first messenger to touch lunar soil.
moon.howItWorked: Ballistic impact probe.
moon.scienceLegacy: Demonstrated trans-lunar trajectory tracking accuracy.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Far side crater coordinates mapped by LROC.
keyFacts: First American spacecraft to touch the Moon (April 26, 1962).
Impacted at 9,600 km/h on the lunar Far Side.

moon.name: Ranger 7 Impact Site
moon.brief: Transmitted 4,308 breathtaking close-up television photographs as it plunged toward the Moon, transforming human understanding of lunar craters.
moon.description: After six consecutive Ranger failures, Ranger 7 broke the curse. During its final 17 minutes of flight, its six vidicon cameras transmitted 4,308 photographs with 1,000 times greater resolution than any Earth telescope. The plain was officially renamed Mare Cognitum («The Sea That Has Become Known»).
moon.whyAbandoned: Intentional high-speed photographic plunge.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: For seventeen minutes, I opened human eyes to the true face of the Moon. Falling at ten thousand kilometers an hour, I sent four thousand frames of crater rims and boulders rushing upward, right up to the final split second before impact.
moon.howItWorked: Six vidicon television cameras capturing full-scan and partial-scan images in rapid succession.
moon.scienceLegacy: Proved the Moon was cratered down to millimeter scales and cleared the way for the Surveyor and Apollo landing designs.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Impact crater identified in Mare Cognitum by LROC.
keyFacts: First US mission to successfully transmit close-up pictures of the lunar surface.
The International Astronomical Union named the impact sea Mare Cognitum in its honor.

moon.name: Ranger 8 Impact Site
moon.brief: Transmitted 7,137 high-resolution photographs of Mare Tranquillitatis, directly scouting the future landing zone of Apollo 11.
moon.description: Ranger 8 slammed into the Sea of Tranquility on February 20, 1965, sending photos down to the final 23 minutes of its plunge. Its imagery allowed Apollo mission planners to select smooth candidate landing zones for Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin.
moon.whyAbandoned: High-speed photographic impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I plummeted into the Sea of Tranquility four years before Eagle arrived, mapping every ridge and crater to ensure the first footprints would land on safe ground.
moon.howItWorked: Six vidicon cameras transmitting across two independent television channels.
moon.scienceLegacy: Directly mapped the landing safety corridor for Apollo 11 Tranquility Base.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: LROC identified the Ranger 8 impact crater and dark ejecta halo.
keyFacts: Returned 7,137 high-resolution photographs of the Apollo 11 region.
Impacted at 2.68 km/s (9,650 km/h).

moon.name: Ranger 9 Impact Site
moon.brief: Targeted directly into the central peak of crater Alphonsus, broadcast live on American network television to millions of viewers.
moon.description: Ranger 9’s final plunge was converted directly into standard commercial television format and broadcast live on CBS, NBC, and ABC, letting millions of viewers watch the crater floor rush up until the screen snapped to static upon impact.
moon.whyAbandoned: Live television impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: Millions of people on Earth watched through my eyes as the central peak of Alphonsus Crater rushed up to fill their living room television screens.
moon.howItWorked: Scan conversion technology translating scientific camera signals to commercial NTSC television in real time.
moon.scienceLegacy: Proved the volcanic origin of dark-halo impact craters inside Alphonsus.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Impact crater on the floor of Alphonsus confirmed by LROC.
keyFacts: First spacecraft impact broadcast live on national television.
Transmitted 5,814 images before impact.

moon.name: Lunar Orbiter 1 Deorbit Site
moon.brief: The spacecraft that took the historic first photograph of Earth rising above the lunar horizon, intentionally crashed to avoid radio interference with Apollo.
moon.description: On August 23, 1966, Lunar Orbiter 1 pointed its camera back toward home and captured the very first image of Earth floating above the lunar landscape. After mapping 5 million square kilometers of surface to select Apollo landing sites, it was commanded to fire its engine and crash into the Far Side to prevent interference with Lunar Orbiter 2.
moon.whyAbandoned: Controlled deorbit impact to preserve radio frequencies.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I turned my lens away from the craters and saw something breathtaking: our blue and white Earth, fragile and glowing, rising above the desolate gray rim of the Moon. When my mission was complete, I was guided into the Far Side to sleep.
moon.howItWorked: Self-contained Eastman Kodak 70mm film camera laboratory that exposed, chemically developed, and scanned film electronically in orbit.
moon.scienceLegacy: Captured the historic first «Earthrise» photograph and surveyed the initial primary Apollo landing sites.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Far side impact location mapped by LROC.
keyFacts: Captured the first photograph of Earth as seen from the vicinity of the Moon (August 23, 1966).
Developed real photographic film inside an automated mini-darkroom in lunar orbit.

moon.name: Lunar Orbiter 2 Deorbit Site
moon.brief: Famed for taking the dramatic oblique photograph of Copernicus crater heralded worldwide as the «Picture of the Century».
moon.description: Surveyed potential Apollo landing sites and returned the stunning telephoto view of Copernicus crater’s central peaks and 3,000-meter cliffs. Deliberately crashed into the Far Side on October 11, 1967.
moon.whyAbandoned: Controlled deorbit impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I tilted my camera across the jagged maw of Copernicus crater, revealing mountains rising from its floor that looked like a landscape from a science fiction novel.
moon.howItWorked: High-resolution Eastman Kodak dual-lens camera and readout scanner.
moon.scienceLegacy: Provided the first three-dimensional topographical perspective of giant impact crater morphologies.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Identified by LROC on the Far Side.
keyFacts: Its oblique photo of Copernicus was hailed by newspapers worldwide as the «Picture of the Century».
Mapped 13 candidate Apollo landing zones.

moon.name: Luna 5 Impact Site
moon.brief: A 1.5-ton early Soviet soft-landing attempt that crashed into the Sea of Clouds when its retrorockets failed to fire.
moon.description: During descent, a flotation gyroscope failure in the I-100 guidance system prevented proper attitude hold, and the retrorocket failed to ignite.
moon.whyAbandoned: High-speed surface impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: My gyroscopes tumbled in the dark, and my braking engines stayed cold. I struck the Sea of Clouds at three kilometers per second.
moon.howItWorked: Early KTDU-5A retrorocket descent module.
moon.scienceLegacy: Taught Soviet engineers the gyroscopic stabilization redundancies needed for the historic Luna 9 success.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Mare Nubium impact zone verified by LROC.
keyFacts: Weighed 1,476 kg at impact.
One of several developmental test flights that enabled the Luna 9 triumph.

moon.name: Luna 20 Descent Stage
moon.brief: The robotic lander that soft-landed in the mountainous Apollonius highlands and returned 55 grams of pristine ancient anorthosite to Earth.
moon.description: While Luna 16 sampled the dark mare basalt, Luna 20 proved that Soviet robotic craft could navigate and touch down in treacherous mountain highlands. Its drill bored through tough rock, returning 55 grams of ancient anorthosite feldspar.
moon.whyAbandoned: Descent stage left as launch platform.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I landed between the craters of the Apollonius mountains. My drill bit chewed through stone older than the solar system, sending white anorthosite crystals back to Moscow.
moon.howItWorked: Rotary-percussion diamond drill capable of penetrating hard highland breccias.
moon.scienceLegacy: Directly confirmed that the lunar highlands are composed predominantly of anorthosite feldspar, matching Apollo 15's findings.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed in high resolution in the Apollonius highlands by LROC.
keyFacts: First robotic spacecraft to successfully return highland rocks to Earth.
Returned 55 grams of lunar crustal material.

moon.name: Luna 23 Damaged Lander
moon.brief: A sample-return lander that tipped over on a boulder during touchdown in Mare Crisium, damaging its drill and preventing sample launch.
moon.description: On November 6, 1974, Luna 23 touched down on unfavorable, rough terrain in southern Mare Crisium. The spacecraft tipped over onto its side upon landing, damaging its core drill mechanism and making ascent stage launch impossible.
moon.whyAbandoned: Vehicle tipped over upon touchdown; transmitted engineering data for 3 days.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I landed upon a field of boulders in Mare Crisium. A rock caught my leg, and I tipped sideways onto the dust. My drill could not reach the ground, and my rocket could never fly.
moon.howItWorked: Deep-core 2.5-meter drill assembly.
moon.scienceLegacy: Led to site redesign and landing radar upgrades that ensured the complete success of Luna 24 two years later just 2.3 km away.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Rediscovered in March 2012 by LROC NAC, confirming that the lander was indeed lying on its side.
keyFacts: Lies just 2.3 km from the successful Luna 24 landing site.
Confirmed by LROC photographs to be resting on its side.

moon.name: Luna 25 Crash Site
moon.brief: Russia’s first lunar mission in 47 years, which crashed into Pontécoulant crater following an engine overburn during orbit lowering.
moon.description: On August 19, 2023, while executing a planned thruster burn to lower its orbit before attempting a soft landing near the south pole, the propulsion system fired for 127 seconds instead of the planned 84 seconds due to an accelerometer unit data communication error, driving the probe directly into the inner rim of Pontécoulant G crater.
moon.whyAbandoned: Engine overburn caused orbital collision.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: Forty-seven years after Luna 24, I carried the name of the great Soviet lunar probes back to the Moon. But an engine burn lasted forty-three seconds too long, and I crashed into the southern mountains.
moon.howItWorked: Pulsed liquid-propellant landing engines with laser hazard sensors.
moon.scienceLegacy: Provided new impact flash calibration data for orbital observatories.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed by LROC just days after impact, revealing a brand-new 10-meter crater on the steep inner rim of Pontécoulant G crater.
keyFacts: Created a new 10-meter diameter impact crater detected by NASA's LRO.
Russia's first lunar probe since Luna 24 in 1976.

moon.name: Hiten & Hagoromo Impact Sites
moon.brief: Japan’s first lunar probe, which pioneered low-energy gravity-assist trajectories before deliberately impacting near Stevinus crater.
moon.description: Launched in 1990 by Japan's ISAS, Hiten pioneered chaotic orbit transfers using Earth-Moon Lagrange points (developed by Edward Belbruno). On April 10, 1993, after completing hundreds of orbits, it was commanded to impact the lunar surface.
moon.whyAbandoned: Controlled deorbit impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I brought Japan to the Moon through the invisible currents of gravity. Using the gentle pull of the Earth and the Sun, I drifted into lunar orbit with scarcely a drop of fuel, touching down in the dust near Stevinus.
moon.howItWorked: Pioneered low-energy ballistic capture trajectories now widely used by commercial lunar missions.
moon.scienceLegacy: Revolutionized astrodynamics and trajectory optimization.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Impact region verified near Stevinus crater by LROC.
keyFacts: Made Japan the third nation to place an artificial satellite in lunar orbit.
Pioneered low-energy gravity-assist orbital mechanics.

moon.name: SMART-1 Impact Site
moon.mission: Small Missions for Advanced Research in Technology
moon.brief: Europe’s first mission to the Moon, propelled by an innovative solar-electric ion engine that gently spiraled across space for 14 months.
moon.description: Using just 82 kg of xenon gas, SMART-1’s Snecma PPS-1350 Hall-effect ion engine gently pushed the spacecraft into lunar orbit. On September 3, 2006, after mapping lunar chemical elements with an X-ray spectrometer, it grazed into Lacus Excellentiae at a shallow 1-degree angle at 2 km/s.
moon.whyAbandoned: Deliberate low-angle impact to observe lunar flash and ejecta from Earth.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: With a whisper of blue xenon ion gas, I carried the flag of Europe to the Moon. I skimmed into the Lake of Excellence like a flat stone skipping across water, my impact flash observed by telescopes across the world.
moon.howItWorked: Solar-electric ion propulsion accelerating xenon ions at 16 km/s using electricity generated by solar arrays.
moon.scienceLegacy: Mapped calcium, silicon, and aluminum in the lunar crust using the D-CIXS X-ray spectrometer.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Impact scar and ricochet furrow identified in Lacus Excellentiae by LROC.
keyFacts: First European spacecraft to orbit and impact the Moon.
Impact flash was observed live by the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope.

moon.name: Chandrayaan-1 Moon Impact Probe (MIP)
moon.statusLabel: First Water Discovery at South Pole (2008)
moon.brief: The probe that discovered water molecules in the thin lunar atmosphere during its 25-minute descent into the south polar Shackleton crater.
moon.description: Ejected from the Chandrayaan-1 orbiter on November 14, 2008, the 34 kg Moon Impact Probe plummeted into the south pole near Shackleton crater. Its quadrupole mass spectrometer (CHACE) recorded 650 mass spectra during the descent, directly detecting water molecules in the exosphere before crashing.
moon.whyAbandoned: Kinetic impact exploration.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was India’s first touch upon the lunar south pole. As I fell toward the black abyss of Shackleton Crater, my spectrometer tasted water vapor rising from the permafrost, proving to the world that the poles are rich with ice.
moon.howItWorked: Quadrupole mass spectrometer analyzing exospheric gas species during freefall descent.
moon.scienceLegacy: Directly verified water molecules in the polar lunar atmosphere, corroborated by NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M3).
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Shackleton crater rim surveyed by LROC.
keyFacts: First Indian object to touch the Moon (November 14, 2008).
The impact point was named «Jawahar Point» by the Indian government.

moon.name: Kaguya (SELENE) Impact Site
moon.brief: The 3-ton Japanese lunar explorer that beamed the world’s first full-HD videos of Earthrise before crashing near Gill crater.
moon.description: Equipped with 14 scientific instruments and high-definition television cameras, Kaguya mapped lunar gravity, surface elemental composition, and discovered giant lava tubes that could house future underground lunar bases. It was deorbited into the surface on June 10, 2009.
moon.whyAbandoned: Controlled deorbit impact at end of mission.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I shared the beauty of the Moon with humanity in glorious high definition—flying over crater rims and broadcasting crystal-clear views of Earth floating in the void.
moon.howItWorked: Dual subsatellites (Okina and Ouna) for four-way Doppler gravity mapping.
moon.scienceLegacy: Discovered underground lunar lava tubes hundreds of meters wide in the Marius Hills region.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Impact site and debris streak photographed near Gill crater by LROC.
keyFacts: Brought the world the first High-Definition Television (HDTV) footage of the Moon.
Discovered skylights into massive subterranean lava tubes suitable for future human habitats.

moon.name: LCROSS Shepherding Spacecraft Impact
moon.brief: Flew directly through the debris plume kicked up by the Centaur rocket, analyzing water ice spectra in real-time before impacting 4 minutes later.
moon.description: Following four minutes behind the Centaur impactor, the shepherding spacecraft turned its nine spectrometers, radiometers, and cameras toward the rising dust cloud in Cabeus crater, streaming conclusive infrared fingerprints of water before slamming into the crater itself.
moon.whyAbandoned: Terminal impact flight path.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I flew into the plume my companion rocket created, tasting the vaporized dust of Cabeus crater. In my final four minutes of flight, my spectrometers confirmed the signature of pure water ice before I plunged into the dark alongside the Centaur.
moon.howItWorked: Near-infrared and mid-infrared spectrometers detecting 1.4 and 1.9 micrometer water absorption bands.
moon.scienceLegacy: Confirmed pure water ice, methane, ammonia, and hydrocarbons trapped in permanently shadowed craters.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Cabeus crater floor surveyed by LROC and DIVINER.
keyFacts: Flew directly through the impact cloud to measure water absorption bands.
Confirmed that the lunar south pole contains billions of tons of accessible water ice.

moon.name: GRAIL «Ebb» & «Flow» Impact Site
moon.brief: Twin spacecraft that mapped the Moon’s gravitational field with unprecedented precision, crashed side-by-side into a mountain named after Sally Ride.
moon.description: Ebb and Flow orbited in tandem, measuring micro-meter changes in distance between each other to create the highest-resolution gravity map of any planetary body. Running out of fuel on December 17, 2012, both probes impacted a mountain near Goldschmidt crater at 1.7 km/s. NASA officially named the impact site in honor of first American woman in space, Sally Ride.
moon.whyAbandoned: Controlled deorbit into non-historic highland mountain.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: We were twins, flying in formation over craters and mountains to weigh the heart of the Moon. When our fuel was spent, we dove side-by-side into a polar mountain named after Sally Ride.
moon.howItWorked: Microwave Ka-band ranging system measuring inter-spacecraft distance variations down to a fraction of a micron.
moon.scienceLegacy: Revealed that the lunar crust was thoroughly fractured by ancient impacts and much thinner than previously thought (34–43 km thick).
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Both distinct impact craters photographed side-by-side by LROC NAC.
keyFacts: Produced the highest-resolution gravity map of any body in the solar system.
The impact mountain was officially named «Sally K. Ride Impact Site» by NASA.

moon.name: LADEE Deorbit Site
moon.mission: Lunar Atmosphere and Dust Environment Explorer
moon.brief: Investigated whether levitating charged dust creates the mysterious pre-dawn horizon glows reported by Apollo astronauts, impacting on the Far Side.
moon.description: Demonstrated high-speed optical laser communications with Earth (622 Mbps) and sampled the ultra-thin lunar exosphere and levitating dust particles. On April 18, 2014, it impacted the eastern rim of Sundman V crater on the lunar Far Side at 5,800 km/h.
moon.whyAbandoned: Planned high-speed deorbit impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I investigated the ghostly glow that Apollo astronauts saw rising above the lunar horizon before dawn. My dust sensors counted the levitating grains of regolith lofted by electrostatic charge, until I dove into Sundman Crater on the Far Side.
moon.howItWorked: Laser Dust Experiment (LDEX) and Neutral Mass Spectrometer analyzing tenuous lunar exosphere gases.
moon.scienceLegacy: Characterized the fragile neon, helium, and argon exosphere of the Moon.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged by LROC on the rim of Sundman V crater.
keyFacts: Pioneered ultra-high-speed laser communications from lunar orbit (622 megabits/sec).
Confirmed the presence of neon, argon-40, and helium in the tenuous lunar atmosphere.

moon.name: Beresheet Crash Site
moon.brief: The world’s first privately funded mission to attempt a soft landing on the Moon, crashing into Mare Serenitatis after an IMU reset shutdown its main engine.
moon.description: Built by Israeli non-profit SpaceIL, Beresheet flew to the Moon on an ultra-low-budget rideshare profile. During final descent at 150 meters altitude, an inertial measurement unit (IMU) failed. A computer restart shut off the main braking engine, and the craft crashed into Mare Serenitatis at 500 km/h, scattering an archive that famously included microscopic dehydrated tardigrades.
moon.whyAbandoned: Main engine failure at 150 meters altitude during landing.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was built on dreams and crowdfunding, the first private mission to reach for the lunar surface. Seconds before touchdown in the Sea of Serenity, my engine flickered and died. I struck the dust at five hundred kilometers an hour, leaving an archive of human knowledge and resilient tardigrades asleep in the soil.
moon.howItWorked: Low-cost commercial spacecraft using off-the-shelf components and monopropellant thrusters.
moon.scienceLegacy: Pioneered the commercial lunar exploration paradigm, leading to NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed in Mare Serenitatis by NASA's LROC, showing a distinct dark impact smudge with a 100-meter ray system.
keyFacts: First privately funded spacecraft to reach lunar orbit.
Carried a 30-million-page digital archive and dehydrated tardigrades («water bears»).

moon.name: Chandrayaan-2 «Vikram» Impact Site
moon.brief: India’s first attempt to land at the south pole, which crashed during the «fine braking» phase at 2.1 km altitude.
moon.description: On September 6, 2019, Vikram began its automated descent towards the south polar region. During the fine braking phase 2.1 km above the surface, thrust variations caused the craft to deviate from its trajectory and lose radio contact. The wreckage was spotted months later on LROC images by Indian engineer Shanmuga Subramanian.
moon.whyAbandoned: Guidance software software saturation during terminal deceleration.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: Two kilometers above the southern craters, my guidance software lost control of our trajectory. I crashed into the highland boulders, but my failure was the seed from which Chandrayaan-3 achieved total victory four years later.
moon.howItWorked: Five throttleable 800 N liquid engines.
moon.scienceLegacy: The telemetry analysis directly inspired the expanded landing ellipse and reinforced landing legs that made Chandrayaan-3 a triumph in 2023.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Identified on LROC images by amateur space enthusiast Shanmuga Subramanian, later confirmed by NASA and ISRO.
keyFacts: Debris field discovered through citizen science collaboration between LROC and Indian mechanical engineer Shanmuga Subramanian.
Paved the way for India's historic Chandrayaan-3 success.

moon.name: Chang'e 5 Descent Stage
moon.brief: The lander that drilled and scooped 1.73 kg of lunar rocks from the volcanic volcanic dome of Mons Rümker, proving the Moon was volcanically active far longer than thought.
moon.description: Touching down on December 1, 2020, near the volcanic volcanic plateau of Mons Rümker in northern Oceanus Procellarum, Chang'e 5 used a robotic shovel and percussion drill to pack 1,731 grams of soil into an ascent rocket, launching back to Earth on December 3.
moon.whyAbandoned: Permanent landing base in Oceanus Procellarum.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I drilled into the young volcanic plain near Mons Rümker. My samples proved that volcanic fires still burned inside the Moon just two billion years ago—a billion years longer than scientists had ever believed.
moon.howItWorked: High-speed automated robotic arm with integrated soil carousel and percussive drill.
moon.scienceLegacy: Dating of its returned samples revealed volcanic basalts just 2.03 billion years old, overturning previous models that the Moon went geologically dead 3 billion years ago.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Photographed in northern Oceanus Procellarum by LROC.
keyFacts: Returned 1,731 grams of lunar soil to Earth on December 16, 2020.
Proved volcanic activity continued on the Moon until at least 2 billion years ago.

moon.name: Hakuto-R Mission 1 Crash Site
moon.brief: Japanese commercial lander carrying the UAE’s Rashid rover, which ran out of fuel while hovering 5 km too high due to a software radar glitch.
moon.description: On April 25, 2023, while descending into Atlas crater, the lander’s onboard computer encountered an unexpected cliff edge. Its altitude software rejected the laser altimeter readings as an error, believing it was 5 km lower than it actually was. The lander hovered until fuel ran out and fell in freefall into Atlas crater.
moon.whyAbandoned: Propellant exhaustion caused by radar altitude software glitch.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I flew as the first private commercial lunar lander from Japan, carrying the Rashid rover from the Emirates. But my radar misjudged a crater rim, and I hovered high in the sky until my fuel ran dry, falling into the silent dunes of Atlas Crater.
moon.howItWorked: Commercial lunar landing architecture designed by ispace.
moon.scienceLegacy: Flight telemetry helped refine radar cliff-edge filtering algorithms for the Hakuto-R Mission 2 lander.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged on the floor of Atlas crater by NASA’s LROC, showing 4 distinct debris patches and a dark surface disturbance.
keyFacts: Carried the UAE's 10 kg Rashid rover and a transformable robot ball.
Crashed into Atlas crater when altitude sensors mistook a crater rim for ground touchdown.

moon.name: Apollo 16 Saturn V S-IVB Impact Site
moon.brief: Fourteen-ton rocket booster impact recorded simultaneously by the Apollo 12, 14, and 15 seismic network.
moon.description: Impacted Oceanus Procellarum at 2.55 km/s on April 19, 1972, providing crucial calibration for seismic stations across thousands of kilometers.
moon.whyAbandoned: Seismic sounding experiment.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was the third of the great Saturn rockets to strike the Moon for science. Three separate ALSEP stations felt my impact reverberating through the rock.
moon.howItWorked: Auxiliary propulsion burn.
moon.scienceLegacy: Mapped the thickness of the lunar crust across the western maria.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Impact crater identified by LROC in Oceanus Procellarum.
keyFacts: Weighed 14,002 kg at impact.
Signals picked up simultaneously by three active Apollo seismometers.

moon.name: Apollo 17 Saturn V S-IVB Impact Site
moon.brief: The final 14-ton Saturn V rocket booster impact in human history, crashing at 2.55 km/s to complete the Apollo seismic map.
moon.description: On December 10, 1972, the Apollo 17 S-IVB stage struck Mare Nubium. The impact was recorded by the full four-station ALSEP network (Apollo 12, 14, 15, and 16), completing humanity’s most comprehensive seismic survey of the lunar interior.
moon.whyAbandoned: Final seismic calibration impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was the last Saturn V rocket stage ever to crash upon the Moon. When I struck the Sea of Clouds, four seismic observatories listened to my final echo, closing the greatest chapter of human lunar exploration.
moon.howItWorked: Kinetic energy impact equal to ~11 tons of TNT.
moon.scienceLegacy: Completed the four-station Apollo Seismic Network triangulation dataset, allowing scientists to determine the Moon's deep core size.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Identified by LROC with an asymmetrical 34-meter crater and ray system.
keyFacts: The final Saturn V rocket stage ever launched in the Apollo program.
Detected simultaneously by four different Apollo ALSEP stations.

moon.name: Apollo 10 LM «Snoopy» Descent Stage
moon.brief: The descent stage of Apollo 10 LM Snoopy, flown down to 14.4 km above the surface in the final dress rehearsal before Apollo 11.
moon.description: Gene Cernan and Tom Stafford flew Snoopy down to within 47,000 feet (14.4 km) of the lunar surface in Mare Tranquillitatis, testing the landing radar and surveying Apollo 11's landing site. The descent stage was separated and its orbit decayed into the Moon.
moon.whyAbandoned: Deorbited into the Moon following rehearsal separation.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I brought human eyes within eight miles of the lunar craters for the first time. We scouted Tranquility Base, confirming that Neil and Buzz could make the landing two months later.
moon.howItWorked: Throttleable hypergolic descent rocket engine (LMDE).
moon.scienceLegacy: Directly verified the lunar landing radar and gravity mascon models for Apollo 11.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Mare Tranquillitatis region mapped by LROC.
keyFacts: Descended to just 14.4 km (47,000 ft) above the lunar surface.
Flew the dress rehearsal that guaranteed Apollo 11's success.

moon.name: Apollo 15 Subsatellite (PFS-1)
moon.brief: A 36 kg hexagonal satellite launched from the Apollo 15 Service Module into lunar orbit, studying magnetic fields and gravitational mascons before crashing in 1973.
moon.description: Spring-ejected from the Apollo 15 Scientific Instrument Module (SIM) bay into lunar orbit on August 4, 1971. It completed 4,250 orbits, mapping lunar magnetic anomalies and gravitational mascons until its orbit decayed into the Far Side on January 15, 1973.
moon.whyAbandoned: Orbital decay impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was a small hexagonal satellite launched from Apollo 15's shoulder. I circled the Moon four thousand times, mapping invisible magnetic ripples until the gravity mascons dragged me down into the Far Side.
moon.howItWorked: Spin-stabilized hexagonal prism with deployable magnetometer booms.
moon.scienceLegacy: Discovered that lunar mascons create chaotic gravitational orbital perturbations.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Far side impact swath mapped by LROC.
keyFacts: Ejected directly from the Apollo 15 spacecraft in lunar orbit.
Completed 4,250 lunar orbits.

moon.name: Apollo 16 Subsatellite (PFS-2)
moon.brief: Ejected into an eccentric orbit that decayed in just 34 days due to intense lunar gravitational mass concentrations (mascons).
moon.description: Released on April 24, 1972, PFS-2 orbited through lunar gravitational anomalies that rapidly altered its orbital periapsis from 97 km down to 10 km. On its 425th orbit on May 29, 1972, it struck the Far Side.
moon.whyAbandoned: Gravitational mascon orbital collapse.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: The strange lumpiness of the Moon's gravity caught me in its grip. With every orbit, the mascons pulled me closer, until after just 425 laps, I smashed into the Far Side mountains.
moon.howItWorked: Magnetometer and charged particle telescope powered by solar cells.
moon.scienceLegacy: Provided the first experimental proof of how severely lunar mascons distort low-altitude orbits.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Far side crater mapped by LROC.
keyFacts: Impacted after only 34 days due to gravitational perturbations.
Demonstrated the hazard of frozen lunar orbits.

moon.name: Lunar Orbiter 3 Deorbit Site
moon.brief: Photographed the Surveyor 1 spacecraft sitting on the lunar surface, proving that orbital cameras could spot robotic probes from space.
moon.description: Lunar Orbiter 3 pinpointed the primary Apollo landing sites and took the historic photo of Surveyor 1 on the ground. Intentionally commanded into a deorbit impact on October 9, 1967.
moon.whyAbandoned: Controlled deorbit impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: From fifty miles above the Moon, my cameras zoomed in on Flamsteed Crater and spotted Surveyor 1 sitting in the dust—the first time one spacecraft had photographed another on the surface of another world.
moon.howItWorked: High-magnification telescopic film camera with onboard bimat processor.
moon.scienceLegacy: Confirmed that Apollo astronauts could be tracked and located from lunar orbit.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Deorbit coordinates cataloged by LROC.
keyFacts: First spacecraft to photograph another manmade probe on another celestial body.

moon.name: Lunar Orbiter 4 Deorbit Site
moon.brief: Mapped 99% of the near side of the Moon in high resolution, creating the foundational atlas used for all Apollo landings.
moon.description: Operated in an elliptical polar orbit, acquiring 546 high-resolution frames that covered virtually the entire visible face of the Moon. Deorbited on October 31, 1967.
moon.whyAbandoned: Controlled deorbit impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I mapped 99 percent of the Moon’s near side, stitching together the photographic atlas that guided humanity’s path to Apollo.
moon.howItWorked: Polar elliptical orbit photography.
moon.scienceLegacy: Formed the baseline cartographic atlas for Apollo, Soviet Luna, and modern Artemis missions.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Impact crater mapped in Mare Fecunditatis by LROC.
keyFacts: Mapped 99% of the near side of the Moon.

moon.name: Lunar Orbiter 5 Deorbit Site
moon.brief: The final Lunar Orbiter, completing high-resolution photographic sweeps of 36 candidate Apollo sites before impacting near the western limb.
moon.description: Photographed pristine scientific targets including Aristarchus crater, Tycho, and the Alpine Valley. Deorbited on January 31, 1968.
moon.whyAbandoned: Controlled deorbit impact.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was the last of the Lunar Orbiters. With my final film rolls, I photographed 36 Apollo target zones and the glowing radioactive plateau of Aristarchus.
moon.howItWorked: Dual-lens 24-inch and 3-inch focal length cameras.
moon.scienceLegacy: Completed NASA's primary photographic exploration phase before Apollo 8 and 11.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Deorbit site mapped by LROC.
keyFacts: Completed reconnaissance for 36 Apollo landing candidates.

moon.name: Luna 7 Crash Site
moon.brief: A 1.5-ton Soviet soft-landing attempt that crashed when optical sensor lock failure caused the retrorocket to shut off prematurely.
moon.description: During descent, the optical star tracker lost attitude lock, triggering premature engine shutdown, and the probe impacted Oceanus Procellarum at 3.2 km/s.
moon.whyAbandoned: Impact crash during terminal deceleration.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I lost sight of Earth in the blackness, and my braking engines stopped. I struck Oceanus Procellarum at ten thousand kilometers an hour.
moon.howItWorked: Early Soviet soft-landing architecture.
moon.scienceLegacy: Led to improved optical tracker baffles for Luna 9.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Oceanus Procellarum impact site verified by LROC.
keyFacts: Impact velocity of 3.2 km/s.

moon.name: Luna 8 Crash Site
moon.brief: The immediate predecessor to Luna 9, crashing when an airbag punctured by a mounting bracket induced an uncontrollable spin.
moon.description: During retrorocket firing, the landing cushioning airbag inflated prematurely, was punctured by a metal bracket, and the outgassing jet sent the probe into a spin. Retrorockets cut off and it impacted Oceanus Procellarum.
moon.whyAbandoned: Airbag puncture caused loss of attitude control.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: A punctured airbag spun me into a flat spin seconds before landing. My sacrifice revealed the bracket flaw that Korolev fixed on Luna 9.
moon.howItWorked: Inflatable landing airbags.
moon.scienceLegacy: Directly solved the final mechanical issue before Luna 9 achieved the world's first soft landing 58 days later.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged in Oceanus Procellarum by LROC.
keyFacts: Direct precursor to the historic Luna 9 landing.

moon.name: Luna 18 Crash Site
moon.brief: Soviet sample-return attempt that crashed into the steep mountain slopes of Mare Fecunditatis.
moon.description: Intended to drill and return highland samples, Luna 18 fired its descent engine on September 11, 1971, but lost altitude hold over steep slopes and crashed.
moon.whyAbandoned: Highland descent terrain collision.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I aimed for the steep highland ridges of Fecunditatis, but the mountain rose faster than my radar could track.
moon.howItWorked: Automated sample return lander.
moon.scienceLegacy: Refined the descent radar profiles for the successful Luna 20 highland landing five months later.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Identified on LROC imagery near Luna 20.
keyFacts: Paved the way for the successful Luna 20 sample return.

moon.name: Chang'e 1 Controlled Impact Site
moon.brief: China’s first lunar orbiter, which created a full 3D stereo map of the Moon before executing a controlled deorbit impact in Mare Fecunditatis.
moon.description: Launched in 2007, Chang'e 1 operated for 16 months, mapping the global distribution of 14 chemical elements and measuring regolith depth with a microwave radiometer. On March 1, 2009, it was commanded to deorbit into Mare Fecunditatis.
moon.whyAbandoned: Controlled deorbit impact at end of mission.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was China’s first step into deep space. For 16 months, I mapped the Moon in 3D stereo, before firing my engines for a planned impact in the Sea of Fertility.
moon.howItWorked: Laser altimeter and stereo camera mapping.
moon.scienceLegacy: Produced China's first comprehensive high-definition 3D lunar surface map.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Mare Fecunditatis impact area mapped by LROC.
keyFacts: China's first lunar exploration mission.
Impact velocity approximately 1.7 km/s.

moon.name: «Fallen Astronaut» Memorial Statuette
moon.statusLabel: Only Art Installation on the Moon
moon.brief: The only artwork on the Moon: an 8.5 cm aluminum figurine and commemorative plaque honoring 14 American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts who died in human spaceflight.
moon.description: Placed discreetly in the regolith by Apollo 15 Commander David Scott at the end of EVA 3, the Fallen Astronaut is an 8.5 cm stylized aluminum statuette designed by Belgian sculptor Paul Van Hoeydonck. Beside it lies a metal plaque bearing the names of 14 space pioneers: Charles Bassett, Pavel Belyayev, Roger Chaffee, Georgi Dobrovolski, Theodore Freeman, Yuri Gagarin, Edward Givens, Gus Grissom, Vladimir Komarov, Viktor Patsayev, Elliot See, Vladislav Volkov, Edward White, and C.C. Williams.
moon.whyAbandoned: Permanent solemn memorial tribute.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I am an eight-centimeter figure of brushed aluminum, resting face-down in the dust of Hadley Rille. Beside me lies a plaque inscribed with fourteen names—seven American, seven Soviet. In the cold vacuum, the politics of the Cold War vanish; I stand as an eternal monument to the men who gave their lives to reach the stars.
moon.howItWorked: Sculpted from solid aerospace aluminum alloy to withstand extreme lunar thermal swings from -170°C to +120°C without oxidizing or degrading.
moon.scienceLegacy: Represents the pinnacle of human artistic and diplomatic memorialization in deep space, uniting both sides of the Space Race.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Recorded in Apollo 15 photography adjacent to the parked Lunar Roving Vehicle.
keyFacts: The only official artwork and sculpture on the surface of the Moon.
Honors both American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts (including Yuri Gagarin and Vladimir Komarov).

moon.name: Alan Shepard's Two Golf Balls
moon.statusLabel: First Sport Played on Another World
moon.brief: Two Wilson golf balls struck with a makeshift 6-iron by Alan Shepard at the conclusion of Apollo 14 EVA 2.
moon.description: At the end of their second moonwalk in Fra Mauro, Alan Shepard pulled a modified 6-iron club head out of his spacesuit pocket, attached it to the handle of a geological contingency sample scoop, dropped two golf balls into the dust, and swung one-handed. He sliced the first into a crater; the second ball flew through the airless vacuum and sailed, in Shepard’s famous words, for «miles and miles and miles».
moon.whyAbandoned: Left on the surface as an iconic piece of space lore.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I flew in the one-sixth gravity of Fra Mauro with no air resistance to slow my spin. Struck by Alan Shepard’s modified six-iron, I sailed across the gray dust and crater rims, resting forever forty yards from the landing stage.
moon.howItWorked: High-energy elastic core designed for golf, benefiting from zero aerodynamic drag and 1/6th Earth gravity.
moon.scienceLegacy: Modern digital image reconstruction by imaging specialist Andy Saunders located the second ball ~40 meters away, proving physical projectile dynamics in lunar vacuum.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Identified through high-contrast reprocessing of Apollo 14 surface photography.
keyFacts: First sports equipment used on another celestial body.
Shepard swung with only his right hand due to the stiffness of his pressurized Apollo spacesuit.

moon.name: Charlie Duke's Family Photograph
moon.statusLabel: Family Portrait on the Lunar Soil
moon.brief: A color photograph of Apollo 16 astronaut Charlie Duke, his wife Dorothy, and their two sons, sealed in plastic and left on the Moon.
moon.description: On April 23, 1972, lunar module pilot Charlie Duke placed a color snapshot of his family on the regolith of Descartes Highlands. On the back, it read: «This is the family of Astronaut Charlie Duke from Planet Earth. Who landed on the Moon, April 1972.» He photographed it with his Hasselblad camera before stepping away.
moon.whyAbandoned: Personal tribute left permanently on the lunar surface.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I was a family photo of Charlie, Dorothy, and their boys sitting on the grass in Houston. Charlie laid me down gently in the gray dust of Descartes Highlands, snapped my picture, and left me under the glare of the cosmic sun.
moon.howItWorked: Kodak photographic paper encased in a protective clear plastic sleeve.
moon.scienceLegacy: A poignant human testament demonstrating that deep-space exploration is driven by families and humanity back on Earth.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Documented in iconic Apollo 16 Hasselblad surface frame AS16-117-18841.
keyFacts: Left by Charlie Duke, the youngest person ever to walk on the Moon (age 36).
The back was signed by Duke’s two young sons, Charles and Thomas.

moon.name: Apollo 11 Goodwill Silicon Message Disc
moon.brief: A coin-sized silicon wafer etched with goodwill messages from presidents, prime ministers, and monarchs of 73 nations, left at Tranquility Base.
moon.description: Manufactured by the Sprague Electric Company, this 3.8 cm silicon disc used micro-electronic etching to shrink statements from 73 world leaders, messages from four US presidents, and a list of congressional leadership by a factor of 660, fitting them onto an indestructible silicon chip.
moon.whyAbandoned: Permanent diplomatic and cultural message from humanity.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: I am no larger than a half-dollar coin, made of pure semiconductor silicon. On my microscopic surface are etched the words of seventy-three world leaders—kings, queens, and prime ministers—wishing for peace as Neil and Buzz stepped into history.
moon.howItWorked: Early semiconductor photolithography etching characters at 1/4 the width of a human hair into ultra-pure silicon oxide.
moon.scienceLegacy: Pioneered micro-photolithographic archival techniques now used for deep-space time capsules.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Rests in the regolith adjacent to the Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle.
keyFacts: Contains goodwill messages from 73 countries, including the UK, France, Japan, India, and Canada.
Manufactured with pioneering microchip photolithography in June 1969.

moon.name: Lunokhod 1 French Laser Retroreflector
moon.brief: A French-built 14-prism silica retroreflector mounted on the nose of Lunokhod 1, lost for 40 years until successfully ranged by laser in 2010.
moon.description: Constructed by Sud-Aviation / CNES in France, this 14-prism retroreflector was mounted on the front chassis of Lunokhod 1. After contact with the rover was lost in 1971, its exact coordinates were unknown until 2010, when NASA's LROC orbiter spotted the rover. In April 2010, the Apache Point Observatory in New Mexico fired a laser at the site and received an astonishingly strong optical echo of 2,000 photons, proving the reflector was still pristine.
moon.whyAbandoned: Passive optical prism array.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: For forty years, I sat in the darkness of Mare Imbrium, forgotten by time. Then, in 2010, an emerald flash from an observatory in New Mexico struck my fourteen prisms. I bounced the photons back to Earth with unmatched strength, telling them: I am still here.
moon.howItWorked: Fourteen fused silica corner-cube prisms arranged in an aluminum housing with silver-coated rear reflection surfaces.
moon.scienceLegacy: Because of its high northern latitude (38.3° N), ranging Lunokhod 1 provides crucial longitudinal and latitudinal balance to the Apollo retroreflector network.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Pinpointed by LROC in March 2010, enabling the successful laser recovery.
keyFacts: Returned 2,000 reflected photons on its very first recovery attempt in April 2010.
Constructed in France during the height of the Cold War as a joint scientific initiative.

moon.name: Lunokhod 2 French Laser Retroreflector
moon.brief: The 14-prism French retroreflector on Lunokhod 2, which has provided laser ranging data to McDonald and Grasse observatories for 50 years.
moon.description: Mounted on the forward bay of Lunokhod 2, this reflector continues to provide lunar distance and libration measurements to international laser stations, operating without any electrical power for half a century.
moon.whyAbandoned: Passive optical retroreflector.
moon.firstPersonMonologue: Mounted on the brow of Lunokhod 2 in Le Monnier crater, I continue my vigil. Every year, pulses of green light from Earth strike my prisms and return home.
moon.howItWorked: Optical retroreflection.
moon.scienceLegacy: Contributes to calculations of lunar tidal dissipation and general relativity verification.
moon.orbitalSpottedBy: Imaged on the rim of Le Monnier crater by LROC.
keyFacts: Continues to return laser reflections to observatories worldwide.
Requires zero battery or electrical power.
